speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: I desire to call the attention of the Minister of Finance (Sir Thomas White) to an item that appears on the front page of this morning's Citizen stating that a Canadian loan of $75,000,000 is being negotiated in New York and that the negotiations are about closed. Is there any truth in this statement?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Negotiations for such a loan have been proceeding for some time past but are not yet concluded. Therefore, any announcement on the subject is premature. My hon. friend is no doubt aware that two years ago we floated in New York a loan of $100,000,000. That loan will mature in August next. The object of the negotiations now in progress is to provide funds to meet that maturity.
Was the forthcoming loan of $75,000,000 covered by the Minister of Finance in that part of his Budget speech referring to the loan of $350,000,000 authorized by resolution?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
No, but loans maturing were referred to in the Budget speech. I stated in that speech that loans were maturing in London and in the United States, and that temporary action would be taken to meet them. There is a resolution now before Parliament asking for the necessary authority to borrow $100,000,000 which covers the amount of loan that we have in view in New York. I stated at the time the $350,000,000 resolution was before the

House that we should require further borrowing legislation.

The minister has stated that the loan of two years ago was for $100,000,000. He now proposes a loan of $75,000,000 to retire it. What becomes of' the difference in amount?
Sir THOMAS' WHITE: A certain proportion of the $100,000,000 has been got in and cancelled.
Is the loan in New York being negotiated privately, or is it being offered for public competition?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The loan is being negotiated through the fiscal agent of the Government, the Bank of Montreal

stagedirection
speechtext:
House again in committee on Bill No. 158, to provide pensions to, or in respect of, members of the Canadian naval, military, and air forces, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 31-payments to wife under certain conditions.

It has been my experience that occasionally the pension awarded is not anything like commensurate with the injury that the soldier received at the front; and considerable correspondence and a certain amount of controversy has been necessary in order to get a new medical board for the man concerned. I suggest that the minister impress upon the Board of Pension Commissioners the necessity of allowing new medical boards to be held whenever doubt is expressed by a competent medical man as to the fairness of the treatment accorded to a soldier by the board. I do not think it should be necessary in such cases to carry on an extended correspondence. The board have been too strict in this regard. I know that they are trying to carry out their duties as well as they can and that they meet with many difficulties, and I do not wish to offer any captious criticism; but I think that arrangements should be made, either by the appointment of a travelling medical board or in some other way, to ensure that where a competent medical man considers that a soldier has not been treated fairly, that soldier shall, in short order, get a new medical board to decide upon his disability and the amount of his pension.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I agree with the general principle laid down by the hon. member,
and I believe that will be found to be the policy of the board in carrying out this law. The organization has been passing through a transition stage, and now that legislation has been passed and the organization completed, I have no doubt that that will be the policy.-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Section agreed to.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish to point out, Mr. Chairman, that so much conversation is going on that it is difficult even to hear the hon. member for Kingston (Mr. Nickle) when he calls out "Carried".
On section 33-pension to unmarried wife at discretion of commission.

Suppose the case of a man who was married in Canada and had lived with his wife a couple of years; then deserted her, went to the United States and lived with another woman there, but did not marry her. In the case of his being killed at the front and of both women claiming pension, which claim would prevail?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Each case would be investigated on its merits by the Pension Board. Subsection 3 of section 33 reads:
A woman who, although not married to the member of the forces, was living with him in Canada at the time he 'became a member of the forces and for a reasonable time previously thereto, and who, at such time, was publicly represented by him as his wife shall, for the purposes of this Act, be considered to have been his unmarried wife, and may, in the case of his death and in the discretion of the commission, [DOT]be awarded a pension equivalent to the pension she would have received had she been his legal widow. The commission may also award a pension if, in its opinion, an injustice would be done by not recognizing a woman as the wife of a member of the forces although there is no evidence that she had been publicly represented by him as his wife.
Section 37 of the Bill gives the 'Commission discretion if the womarf lived in Canada to deal with such a case as my hon. friend mentions. It reads:
The commission may, in its discretion, apportion a pension between several pensionable applicants. Any such award may from time to time be reviewed and varied. Upon the discontinuance or reduction of a pension to one such pensioner, the pension awarded to any other such pensioner may, in the discretion of the comm ssion, be continued or increased, provided the total pension paid to the several pensioners does not exceed the amount prescribed in the Schedules to this Act.
There are a number of case^ of this kind, and they present very grave difficulties. The conclusion embodied in the Bill was the best conclusion that the Committee could reach. The Pension Board, upon in-

vestigating the whole case, might award the pension to one or the other, or might apportion it between the two, as the merits would appear to demand.
May I call attention to the fact, Mr. Chairman, that a kind of soviet is being conducted in this part of the Chamber which is interfering with our hearing the proceedings?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. This is the second time this morning that the attention of the Chair has been directed- to the fact that there is too much conversation in the Chamber. There is a very considerable number of members here; it is not necessary for all hon. gentlemen to remain in order that there shall be a quorum, and I ask hon. members who desire to carry on conversation to repair to the corridors.
They might be sent to the Tower, if there was one.

I see a source of grave difficulty in the application of subclause 3, as explained by the President of the Council. I have in mind now a case bearing on this particular subclause. A soldier has a wife and two children living in Renfrew; he has deserted his wife, and he is at present living with a woman in the United States, and no doubt he 'will parade this woman as his unmarried wife. In 'the event of that soldier's death, who is entitled to the pension? Certainly, by all the laws of fairness and equity, his legal wife and children should be entitled to the pension in that case. If this clause passes, in the shape in which it is and explained by the President of the Council, the money may go to the woman whom he claims to be his unmarried wife.
No.
That is the explanation I have.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
My hon. friend will see that in the particular case he mentions, this clause would have no application, because in the case mentioned, the case of disability
I perhaps inadvertently in my former statement put it a little broader than the circumstances required-the pension is paid to the soldier.
But in the case of death.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the case of death the Board of Pension Commissioners would inquire into all the facts and would deal with the case as its merits would appear to require.
[Mr. Rowell. 1
I understood the minister to say that they would divide the pension.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: They have the power to do it in the case of death.
That is absolutely unfair.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Most serious and complicated questions come before the board, as all military men know, and it is difficult to lay down hard-and-fast rules that will assure justice in all cases; and past experience would appear to indicate that the wisest course is to give some discretion in cases of that kind to the Board of Pension Commissioners. That was the view of the committee.
The subclause reads "was living with him in Canada." So this would not apply to the case of a man living in the United States at the time of enlistment.
'Supposing a soldier is married; a divorce is obtained against him; the .soldier remarries, and then he dies. To whom shall the pension go? To the first or to the second wife?
To the first wife if there is any alimony.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Subclause 4 of this clause says:
A woman who has been divorced or legally separated from a member of the forces who has died shall not .be entitled to a .pension unless she was awarded alimony or an alimentary allowance, in which case she shall be entitled if she is in a dependent condition to the equivalent of the widow's pension or to the equivalent of the alimony or alimentary allowance which was awarded her, whichever is the smaller in amount.
That would 'be the first wife?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
The balance could go to the second wife.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

Why should there be a division with the first wife who has obtained a divorce, surely, on legitimate grounds against the husband? The husband remarries, and he dies. Who is legally and morally entitled to the pension? Assuredly the first wife, and there should be no division with the second. The second may be only the paramour of that man. This is encouraging vice. Let my hon. friend think over the matter.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
You could not deprive the legal wife, the wife who under the law of

the land is his wife, with whom he may be living at the time of his death, of her pension. In the case suggested by my, hon. friend, he says we might intervene, but on what ground could we deprive her of her pension? We would have to pass on the character of every wife, in the case of the second wife.
Mr. LEIMI'EUX: My hon. friend is too pious not to see the difference in the two oases. I am serious in the matter. Here is [DOT]the first wife who has obtained, for cause, a divorce against her husband, .probably and possibly-and let us take it for granted- because he was committing adultery with this woman who becomes his second wife. A divorce is granted; he marries his paramour; then he dies. By what law, moral or otherwise, will you pay the pension to the paramour because she had gone through the ceremony of marriage, which certainly she did not consider as a sacrament but purely as a contract that could be broken at any given moment. The first wife is living; she is an honest, respectable woman, and yet the pension will be divided between her and the paramour. This is creating a very strange state of affairs in society.
If the hon. member were a pension commissioner, what would he do in that case?
I would pay the pension to the honest wife. By all moral law, you cannot do otherwise.

If that is what the hon.
member would do, if he were a commissioner, that is probably what the commissioners will do, and that is why I would support the proposal, especially as clause 37 gives discretion to the commissioners to do the very thing which the hon. gentleman himself would do if he were a commissioner.

Surely my hon. friend will not give any discretionary powers when morally and conscientiously no other course can be taken than the one I have mentioned. Why should 1 leave a discretionary power to a commissioner, that he shall pay, if he so pleases, either to the honest woman, the woman who has been wronged, or to the paramour who has been the cause of all the misfortune that has happened to the honest woman and who probably has been the cause that the children have been scattered amongst other families or in refuges? Surely my hon. friend will reconsider that.
The honourable gentleman is constructing a hypothetical case.

It is happening every
day.

My hon. friend becomes very sympathetic with the victim whom he describes. Men of experience know that there will be for the consideration of this commission a thousand and one cases with different slants of sentiment, and sympathy, and morals, and justice, and right, which this Parliament cannot now foresee; and in order that pure and simple justice may be done, I should much prefer that discretion be given to the commissioners who, it may be presumed, will be men of discernment, rather than try now to build up a law on a series of hypothetical cases. The question as to whose wife shall she be or whose husband shall he be, who shall receive a pension, sounds extremely familiar.
I remember, in the Scriptures, the Saviour was asked on one occasion whose wife should she be after she had married seven brothers, and I do not know quite what the answer was. I do not think there was one.
There was one.
What was the answer?

They neither marry nor
are given in marriage in Heaven.

There the Saviour was laying down a law to cover cases which he foresaw would arise. We cannot legislate for every possible case, but if we secure the right kind of men for commissioners and give them discretionary power in cases of this kind, I think we can trust them to do justice.

In such a case as cited, where the legitimate wife and her children are living, the board should have no discretionary powers. The legitimate wife should share the pension with no other woman in the land. If a man abandons his legitimate wife and children the pension should still go to her.

It is not as simple to give decisions in reference to the complex marriage relations that exist as hon. gentlemen seem to think. My hon. friend (Mr. Marcil) takes a position diametrically opposed to that taken by my hon. friend (Mr. Lemieux). He says the legitimate wife should get the pension and not share it with the other wife. Now if a woman has secured a divorce from her husband she no longer is his legitimate wife, and even if he has gone

through a form of marriage with the paramour who was the cause of the divorce being granted, she is. the legitimate wife because the law recognizes as the wife of the man the woman to whom he has been married, his first wife having been divorced.
The hon. member (Mr. (Lemieux) cited a case where the man obtained the divorce, not the woman.

The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) cited the case of an honest woman securing a divorce from her husband, who then marries the woman who was the cause of the divorce, and he took the position that the pension should be paid to the woman whom I would call the first wife.
The honest woman.

That is one instance. Let me give another instance. A wife deserts her husband and lives with another man, with the result that the husband obtains a divorce from her and marries an honest woman. To whom then should the pension be paid? Certainly it would appear that it should be paid to the woman who was the legal, wife of that man. My inquiries into these questions have led me to the conclusion that the complexity of modern social life, and the disclosures which the war has made, necessitates discretionary power in regard to these domestic conditions being left to the Board of Pension Commissioners, who in each case will have to inquire carefully into the merits surrounding the domestic conditions, and on the wisdom of their administration must rest the satisfactory operation of this Act. You cannot build this Act up on individual cases, because if you do, it will break down, for the complexity of social conditions as disclosed by this war absolutely overwhelms a man. If your Pension Commissioners are not big enough men, if .they have not the qualifications which Solomon is alleged to have had, this Act will break down; but if you get the right men and they enter into the spirit of the Act the legislation will be effective. If you itry to build it up on a consideration of the peculiar circumstances of each individual case the Act will be found to be unworkable and impracticable.

I certainly respect the views of my hon. friend (Mr. Nickle), as he well knows. If we are going to act on the point of view of my hon. friend (Mr. Griesbach) that Christ did not indicate who was the wife, we shall be going to the very root of Christianity. But this is not the time to discuss the question of divorce, al-
though it is engrafted on this subject incidentally. I say that the pension should go to the honest woman, and to the legitimate children in all cases.
The children always get it.

They would not get it
in the case I cited a moment ago.
Oh yes, both sets of children would get it.

I do not know if I am exaggerating, I speak the thought of the moment, but it seems to me that this is putting a,premium on immorality instead of recognizing the services that have been rendered by our gallant men. We must not give way to the whims and passions of men. We must stand by the moral law of the land. My hon. friend (Mr. Griesbach) seems to think that because we had a war and social conditions have changed we must not be too particular about these matters, and must leave discretionary power in the hands of the commissioners. I have the highest regard for the commissioners; I know the Government will appoint the right men; they will not appoint pagans but Christians. But at the same time I do not want to leave discretionary power in their hands if in certain cases they give preference to the paramour.
Oh, no.
Yes, you give preference to the paramour in the case I have cited.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Would my hon. friend permit me to point out one consideration? He objects to giving the board discretionary power.

In such a case as I
have cited.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
In the case mentioned,
who is to decide whether the woman is a paramour or not? Who is to decide the degree of guilt? Suppose we put in such a qualification as my hon. friend suggests.

There will be either a
judgment of the court or a Divorce Act passed by this House, giving power to remarry. The commissioners will know ab initio who is the guilty party.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Quite so, but I am speaking of the legal wife. The man marries again, as he is authorized to do by the decree of divorce. Who is to determine the character of the legal wife, as to whether

she should or should not be disentitled to the pension? My hon. friend will see that to carry out his own suggestion there must be discretionary power left somewhere to determine such a case, and the more he looks at it the clearer he will see the wisdom of the decision of the committee to leave the matter in the hands of the Pension Commissioners.

I would not leave it to the discretion of the commissioners. I would make a law providing that the honest wife, divorced at her request, and divorced by reason of the conclusions arrived at on the evidence-that she with her children should get the pension.

The hon. member (Mr. Lemieux) raises a point to which I take exception. He spoke of the " guilty " person, whether the husband, the first wife, or the second wife. Now, no matter which of them is the guilty one, I submit that the children that are born, whether legitimate or illegitimate, are not guilty parties and should be looked after by the pension commissioners.

It appears to me that the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) would lead the committee into a discussion of questions we could not possibly settle. He is confusing his thoughts on morality with his thoughts on legality. If we were to go into the moral and Christian aspect of the question, I could make out a very Christian case against the woman whom he describes as the honest -woman. Christianity says that people must forgive seventy times seven, and that, I think, would teach the woman that on strictly Christian principles she should have forgiven her husband and not divorced him. When the woman has divorced her husband she has put herself, by her own act, in the legal .position of no longer being his wife. May I. say to my hon. friend that I approximate very closely to his views on the religious side of the question, but that they do not appertain here. The question is as to the legal wife, the husband himself having been divorced contrary to the Christian injunction of forgiveness. The question is not one of morality at all, but of legality: Who is the legal wife of the man? The second wife is his legal wife, according to the laws of the country, and therefore she is entitled to consideration under the Act. May I summarize the situation by repeating that the question is purely and simply one of legality.

I would appeal to my hon. friend's sense of fairness. Let us suppose that he is .a pension commissioner. Now, according to my tenets, I would not favour divorce, but divorce is provided for in our statute-book; it is in the constitution. Any woman can come before the Senate and by giving the necessary evidence she may obtain a divorce. She obtains a divorce, we will assume, and the husband re-marries. He marries the woman who was the cause of the divorce as eternally such a woman has been the cause. As I say, he marries the paramour.
According to law.
Yes; according to law. Now, he dies and the first wife remains with three or four children.
The children are provided for.

Yes, they receive not a very large amount,-a matter that was criticised yesterday. However, the children are provided for. But the mother is there,-the faithful and good wife. Would my hon. friend, as commissioner, take the pension provided in such a case and divide it between the two women, or would he give the whole of the pension to the second wife? May I ask him that question?

I would endeavour, to the best of my ability, to administer the law as it stood. But in the ease of a woman who has cut herself off from a man, I would respect her if she took the position that having divorced him she did not want to have anything further to do with him; and nine out of ten women whom I have met and respected would not care to be supported by such a man.

My hon. friend forgets that during the four years of terrible war that woman, that good and faithful woman, remained at home suffering various anxieties and troubles in bringing up her little ones, whom she protected with her conscience and [DOT]soul, keeping inviolate the home of the absent soldier. She sent that soldier all the little tokens and delicacies which such a wife would send to her good man in the trenches, and now, on his return, she finds that he has been unfaithful. She is by law,-law which we have created and which is on the statute book,- authorized, for her own protection and fair name, to obtain a divorce. She obtains that divorce. Yet my hon. friend would take only the abstract and coldly legal

poinit of view, forgetting the anxieties of the wife and mother, her sufferings and trials during the absence, of that soldier. I am speaking, of course, of the perfect wife, the good, pure, honest, true, Canadian wife. This soldier would not remain in Red Deer nor in Maisonneuve, as the case might be. He would be ashamed of himself and would probably cross the border and establish himself in the United States. If he died, would the Canadian commissioners give the pension do the paramour living on the other side of the boundary, oblivious of the honest and faithful wife? No! My hon. friend, I am sure, would consider the first wife.

As I understand the Act, there would be no discretion in the hands of the commissioners and there would be no other way of doing it. I do not depart from the first sentence I uttered in regard to my hon. friend's attitude. He is mixing up questions of morality and legality, and that is something we cannot carry out in this House. It is impossible to carry it out.
I am very much impressed with my hon. friend's sympathetic references to the sufferings and anxieties of the woman. But if I might give the hon. member, as an old friend, a piece of advice, I would suggest to him not to carry these anxieties too seriously in this world. If he allowed himself to be too much obsessed with anxieties of that kind, I am perfectly Sure they would have a large effect in destroying his ability as a legislator; because, after all, we cannot draw Acts of Parliament along those lines. I think there is the utmost force in the contention that a certain degree of discretion must be left in the hands of the commission.

Just a word in reply to my hon. friend. From my study of law generally and of the fundamentals of Roman law, I may remark that law is founded on morality and not on immorality. Yes, law is founded on morality, and this is a heritage from the old Roman' law. You will find that principle in the common law of England and in the civil laws of countries where any civil law exists.

I quite realize the mental attitude of the hon. member for Maisonneuve in approaching this subject. May I refer to another feature of subsection 3 of section 337 to which I have already called attention, and which leaves absolutely no room for doubt. In the case of an "unmarried wife" there should be no room what-
TMr. Lemieux.]
ever for doubt as to the disposition of funds in the hands of the commissioners. Surely an "unmarried wife" should not obtain any consideration whatever at the hands of the commissioners, and there should be no room for discretion when the married wife is still alive and has dependent children. I have cited the case of a wife with two children, one two years old and the other four.
The hon. member says there should be no room for doubt.
No room for discretion.

Suppose a woman ran away fifteen years ago leaving her husband, and is living in the United States with another man. Suppose ten years ago the husband went to live with another woman and there grew up a family of say, four children. Let us suppose, further, that he volunteered and went to the war and was killed. Does my hon. friend suggest that the woman with the four children should be left to starve in Canada, while the other woman lives in the United States and has not been dependent on the man who was killed ?
My hon. friend misunderstands me. I am referring to the case where the man himself left the woman.
That is not what you said.

Yes, distinctly. He left his wife and went to live with another woman now considered his unmarried wife. His first wife is living in the town of Renfrew with two children. Supposing that man dies to-day, according to this law the commissioners have discretion to divide the funds at their disposal between these two families. There should be no room for doubt in a case of that kind, and the law should not leave any room for doubt. The wife living in Renfrew is undoubtedly entitled to all the funds voted by this Parliament for relieving such a case as that.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the clause carry?
Clause carried on division.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On Section 34-Pension to parent or person replacing parent when dependent. Pension to orphan children cared for by dependent parent or person. Pension to parent or person becoming mentally or physically incapacitated. Pension to such parent or person subject to review, etc.:

I have been requested by the hon. member for South Quebec (Mr. Power) to move this amendment:
That clause 33 of the draft Bill be amended by adding the words " iifcome or " in the forty-fifth line after the words " on account of."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This Bill in its final form is slightly different from the Bill as it waj before the committee at the time, no doubt, when the member for South Quebec framed his amendment. The amendment which my hon. friend has in view would be an amendment to line 6 of clause 34.
iMr. BUREAU: On page 13, after the words " on account of " add the words " income or."

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It would more properly come after the word " her," making the line read " her income or earnings," etc.

That is right. I have no comments to make.
Mr. CHAS. MARCIL: That is to cover the case I brought to the attention of the minister last night. A young man in my constituency who enlisted as a private became a captain and was killed. A pension was given to his mother, and was afterwards taken away because it rwas discovered she had a private income. She explained that her income is barely sufficient to carry along her real estate and that she cannot live without this pension. It is the case of Captain Frank Maguire. I have communicated with the Pension Board, and they seem willing to do something if the law will allow them.

The principle underlying pensions to dependents was the most difficult, I think, that confronted the committee. As the members know, a distinction was made as between the position of the widow of a soldier and the dependent. It was regarded that as a man was legally responsible for the maintenance of his wife, she, as of right, as well as his children, should be entitled to a pension. There is a moral obligation, but not in all the provinces a legal obligation, on a man to support, or assist in the support, of his father and mother, or, using a general expression, " those who may be dependent on him," including sisters and, sometimes, aunts. The committee reached the conclusion that dependents should only be paid a pension when they were dependent on the man who was killed; that is, they had a moral right to look to him for support. To depart from that position would mean that every father-if you include fathers as well 267
as mothers-and mother in the country, as of right, should be entitled to a pension. Arguments were advanced to the committee that where a widowed mother supplemented the allowance to be granted to her by way of pension by her personal earnings, these should not be deducted from the pension allowance. The principle that underlay the granting of pensions to dependents was that the country would give to them sufficient to maintain them in reasonable living conditions. The hon. member for South Quebec was anxious to go further and say that the income of the mother, if not from personal earnings, but from investments, should not be taken into account.. That simply meant that every mother, whether she had one son or ten, and whether she had seen the son that was killed within ten or twelve years or otherwise, would be entitled to a pension. When it was realized that this would cost the country probably $7,000,000 or $8,000,000 a year, and would be, in effect, class legislation of the moslt dangerous character, it was thought inadvisable to make the change. If you lay it down as the principle on which you are granting pensions to dependents that the amount the Government Will grant is sufficient to ensure a reasonable standard of living, then you surely establish the principle that where a widowed mother or another dependent has sufficient means to attain that standard without the pension, no pension should be granted. To say that the personal earnings or income of a dependent shall not be taken into account simply means that the well-to-do in the community -although they may have more in the way of personal income than this committee and the House has determined is a reasonable amount to secure comfortable living-shall have their private income, either from investment or earnings, supplemented hy a Government allowance to the dependent. It would mean that much would be given, relatively speaking, to those who have, and little would be given to those who have not. We felt that it would be bound to produce discord and hard feelings in the country, because one woman who had lost a son and had no other means of support, and had been dependent on him. would get a pension of $48 a month-which by the adoption of this report, Parliament says is sufficient to maintain her-and another woman who has $5,000 of personal income from investments, would also get a pension on the ground that she was entitled to it because she was a dependent. And yet in the same breath the Pension Commissioners



would have to say that an income of $5,000 a year was not sufficient to maintain a woman. We would be led into all sorts of anomalies, and I am afraid great discontent would arise throughout the country. The committee felt they went a long way when they changed the law so that the income from personal employment should not be deducted.
But they felt they were justified in going that far, because if women, in the main women past middle age, cared to devote their energies to increasing the amount they should have to live on, the committee did not feel they would be warranted in deducting that from the pension allowance.

I quite agree with the principle laid down by the hon. gentleman (Mr. Nickle), but he has not covered the case I brought to his attention, which was this: The man in question was killed and the board recognized that his widowed mother, an aged woman, was entitled to a pension. The pension was granted to her and she received it for a year or a year and a half. It was subsequently discovered that this woman had some estate from which she derived a small revenue, only a very small revenue insufficient to meet the exigencies of her situation, and the pension was cut off. I communicated with the Pension Board who stated they were looking further into the matter, and if they found out that the revenue was practically nil the pension would be given back to her-that is, the original pension which was awarded to her in the first place. Now I do not want anything to be inserted in this Bill which would prevent the Pension Board from carrying out that intention.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: There is nothing in the Bill that would prevent that pension from being paid.
That is all I want.

There is a further point to be provided for. We are passing through a transition period. It is possible that to-day a widow may be in receipt of an income which does not entitle her to a pension, but perhaps five years hence that income may fail her.
Then she goes on the pension list.	.
Can she go on in view of the undue limitations that are being imposed?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Yes, the law covers that.
[Mr. Nickle. j

Any time she becomes a
dependent she can get the pension.
On section 40-power to cancel pension of prostitute or adulteress.

Has the question of bigamous marriages been considered in respect to this Bill? I have known several cases of Canadian soldiers who have gone overseas and married, although they had a wife and children in Canada. The soldiers bring those second wives, and the children resulting from the bigamous marriages back to this country and great trouble results. Are such cases as these provided for under the Bill? [DOT]

In such a case the first
wife would get the pension. The overseas woman with whom the soldier had gone through the form of marriage would not be awarded a pension, but the children would.

Under the laws
of this country is a man who has twice married punishable in all the provinces?

That is a long way outside the purport of the Bill. By the provisions of the Criminal Code, as I remember the law, a man who goes through a form of marriage outside of Canada cannot be prosecuted for bigamy, unless he left Canada with the intent to commit bigamy. As the great majority of the men who went overseas and committed bigamy did not leave Canada with that intent-or at least it cannot be so proved-they cannot be punished for bigamy on returning to this country.

I am not sure what the
law is in regard to a matter of that kind, no doubt the lawyers can give an authoritative opinion. Supposing such a man re-marries in England, or in any part of the British Empire, would not the same law apply?

He would be amenable
to the law of England which he broke by going through a form of marriage with a woman, he already being married, but that would not give any jurisdiction to the Canadian courts to try him for that offence.
I need not repeat with respect to this clause the argument we had a moment ago. I think it is an immoral clause and should not be on our statute book.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This clause provides for
exactly what I understood my hon. friend to be arguing for.
Then we are far apart.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The clause provides as
follows:
The pension of any female pensioner who is a common prostitute or who openly lives with any man in a relationship of man and wife without being married to him shall, in the discretion of the commission, be- suspended, discontinued, or cancelled.

I understand the distinction my hon. friend makes, but I am opposed to the discretionary power given here because I say there should be no discretion as between morality and immorality; the Board of Pension Commissioners should not have to exercise its discretion in such matters. My hon. friend is not in bad faith, I know, but that was the gist of my argument. For that consideration- and I am advancing no other-I am opposed to this section, and I ask that a vote be taken on it.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will see that if we were to strike out the clause it would only perpetuate the thing he wishes to avoid, but I assume what the hon. gentleman means is that the pension should be cancelled without any 'discretion in the commission. If my hon. friend wishes to accomplish that he should strike out the words "in the discretion of the commission" rather than strike out the whole clause.
I am not in favour of granting a pension to the adulteress, the paramour, or the prostitute.
The trouble lies in inserting this clause in the Bill. It gives a certain recognition to a condition in society that this committee and this House should not recognize at all in such a way.

This clause puts the Board of Pension Commissioners in the position of a court or a judge. What right has this commission to pronounce upon the moral character of a woman? If some court pronounced upon her morality, it would then be proper for the commission to exercise such discretion; but are they to sit in judgment upon her? Are they to say: From the information we get from our visitors, such and such a woman is not of proper character? I submit that that is a very dangerous practice; it is the practice that I condemned last night.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The point my hon. friend raised last night came before the committee because the clause as originally drafted was broader than this; it contained some such words as "if she was not of good character." In view of the considerations my hon. friend has mentioned, those words were struck out; but the committee did unanimously reachdhe conclusion that if a woman was living as a common prostitute, or if she was openly living with another man as his wife, then it was quite proper to give the Board of Pension Commissioners discretion to terminate the pension. They also had in view the considerations mentioned by the hon. member for Kingston. The committee will agree that the Pensions Committee exercised a wise discretion; they cut out the more general power, and they give the Board of Pension Commissioners power to deal with these two specific cases.
Mr. MjORPHY: I have a good deal of difficulty in feeling that this section is a fair section. A widow might openly live with a man-a widower, say, with children -as his housekeeper, and a kind neighbour might think they were living together as man and wife. In other words, a woman might bb openly living with a man within themeaning of this section, and be assumed to be living with him as his wife; and that

assumption might not be properly founded. It seems to me that this section goes very far towards enabling an imputation to be cast upon an honest woman who has given her husband to the service of the State and who is doing her best to make her way in the world. It would be the next thing to a crime to enable this non-judicial com-missftn to apply to her the odium suggested in this section, simply because she is living in that way.
What does my hon. friend mean "by in. that way?" Is there any other proper way of living but the honest way?

Many a woman lives openly with a man in a domestic way, having her separate apartments in the same house, and perhaps, going out with the man in public. She may be, without remuneration, taking care of a man's children for the sake of having a home. Is she to be stigmatized under any such provision as this?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend misapprehends the effect of the section. It is limited Jo any woman who openly lives with any man in the relationship of man and wife without being married.
What does the minister mean by the words "openly living"? Can a woman be "closedly living" with a man if she is living in the same house with him?

The minister means,
living immorally.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It means the publicly
acknowledged relationship of these two; that they live together as man and wife, and that that is publicly and openly known to the world.
If that is the interpretation, such discretionary powers as are given by this section are undesirable.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext:
How is it to be
"found"?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Wherever you have the word' "found," that means after evidence, after .a hearing and decision.
By the Pension Commissioners, or by a court?

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I am satisfied with
the Pension Commission as a court in that case. .
Mr. ROWELL; I think that my hon. friend's amendment should hardly go so far as to strike out the words "suspended, discontinued or" in the last line; otherwise I see no objection to accepting his suggestion. It is possible that .a woman living in that condition might reform, and it should be possible to restore her pension. I think that the full purpose which my hon. friend has in view would be served if the clause be amended to read as follows, and I so move:
The pension of any female pensioner who is found to ibe a common prostitute or who openly lives with any man in the relationship of man and wife without being married to him shall he suspended, discontinued or cancelled.
Does that make any difference? The commission aJtill use their discretionary power; 'this does not change the purport of the clause.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It becomes their duty to suspend, discontinue or cancel the pension if the facts are found to be as thus indicated.
I should like to have an explanation of the difference between a common prostitute and an unmarried wife. Is there any difference?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.
A common prostitute lives in a bawdy house.
Not necessarily.
There is quite a difference in the Criminal Code.
Or between a private prostitute and an unmarried wife?

As regards the term " unmarried wife," I want to give notice to the minister now that I am going to move on the third reading of this Bill that the term "unmarried wife" disappear from the Bill, and I will give my reasons then.
Amendment agreed to on division.
Section as amended, agreed to on division.

On section 41-pension to cease on marriage, or remarriage:

I object to the phraseology in this clause of " unmarried wife." It seems incongruous that we should introduce into the legislation of this country such a phrase. Whoever heard of an "unmarried" wife? I do not know what the origin of the term is. We had this up the other night, and some clauses were allowed to pass with these words in them, but I think it should be expunged from the other clauses. I do not know whether it is a Yankeeism, or what is is.
It is not a Yankeeism, it is paganism.

No, I think paganism is purer than that. This is worse than paganism. Is it right to the people of Canada to recognize that there is such a thing as an unmarried wife? It is far better to leave this under the old principle of the common law wife, a term used from time immemorial. I should like to know why this committee has departed from that. This term is absurd.

I repeat the protest I have already made. There is only one wife to be recognized, and here we recognize the "unmarried" wife. If the man dies, his pension may be divided between the woman whom he has abandoned and deserted, and the "unmarried" wife with whom he is living. There is discretionary power left to the commission to do that, and that is contrary to the principles held by the Canadian people and will be condemned by all men who have the interest of this country at heart.

I heartily endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Perth North (Mr. Morphy). Nobody should be recognized in common law as an unmarried wife. Such a thing is foreign to our ideas in Canada. If this Bill is passed with these words inserted I at least demand that they be not translated into the French version. When I read as I do " Femme non-inariee " -that is " the limit."

This objection is not a new one. We have from the beginning protested against these immoral clauses in the Bill, and I still protest against them. But I am not surprised at all. An ambiant air has been created since the war began, which shocks the common decency of the people of this country, under the pretext that new social conditions exist. Only yesterday I
was reading a review, which can be found in the reading room and which is published in the good city of Toronto, in which free love is advocated. We are coming to that with this legislation.
I have had to take th'e responsibility for a good deal in reference to this pension legislation, and I am quite prepared to assume the responsibility for coining the expression " unmarried wife."
De-coin it now.
I coined it because there was no other word or language that I could, as a draughtsman, use- to express the idea.
Call her a concubine.

We fnust face conditions as they were disclosed by this war. This war had not been going on for a year before the military departments were confronted, not by scores, but probably by hundreds of women who demanded separation allowance and who were unable to produce their marriage certificates because they had never been married to the men with whom they respectively were living. Years before a domestic relationship had been in existence; the man and the woman had simply gone and lived together, each to the other, although there had been no formal marriage, and children to the number of one, two, three, four and even five had been born. They had a respectable position in the community in which they lived, and nothing would have been known about the irregularity of their former life had not proof been requested whether or not they were married. When the casualties began to pour in, the same condition confronted us who are interested in this pension legislation. What was the status of these women to be? It is all very well to raise one's hands in holy horror and to say that these women should not be recognized and that they and their children should be permitted to starve; but it seems to me you have to go further than that, because if you are prepared to take the position that these women are not entitled to pensions, you simply drive on to. the streets, a woman, who has constantly and regularly been living with a man as his wife, to get a living in the only way she can get it, namely, by selling herself to the man who is willing to buy her. I am not prepared to take that position.

The hon. member is
going off the subject. What we object to as a matter of respect for the dignity of the women to whom we are married, is the

term " unmarried wife." Change the word and we shall not object to paying the money.

I avoided the term
" common law wife," because I did not want to offend the susceptibilities of certain people who would not wish the woman's position in society to be given even that recognition.

She is a concubine at
law.
They would not be prepared to recognize the legal status of a concubine. A man may have half a dozen concubines, but he can only have one common law wife or one unmarried wife.

A definition can be
given.

If any hon. gentleman
can suggest any word that will absolutely express the relationship of a woman having, through a protracted period, constantly been living with one man and not been living with any other, and not having gone through a formal marriage with that man, I would be quite prepared to accept the word.
Mr. MvANION: Why not put in the definition?

There is no such word,
because there is no such thing recognized in the law. Why not say " wife at common law?"
Because many people object to the suggestion.
What do we care if they object? This is worse.

My hon. friend says:
" What do we care if they object?" That is not the position. If the committee, or any member of the committee, can suggest a better word, there is no reason why it should not be incorporated into this legislation. I am taking the responsibility for the language 'because I am responsible for it, and I am telling the committee why I used the word, and I am directing their attention to a condition that has confronted us and that must be faced.
Mr. M'ANION: Why cannot the hon. member put in the definition instead of the word?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I am sorry I must leave the House as I have to catch a train, so I shall have to move that the committee rise, report progress and ask leave to sit again.
[.Hr. Bureau.]
I have been asked by a good many people when the War Purchasing Commission Bill will come before the House again.

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I should say, Monday or Tuesday.
Will it be agreed to bring it up on Tuesday, so that everybody will be relieved?

speakerposition: Minister presiding over the Department of Health; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Tuesday, then.
Progress reported.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
On the motion of Hon. Arthur Meighen (Minister of the Interior) Bill No. 154, to authorize certain School and Dominion Lands to be included in the Taber Irrigation District in the province of Alberta, was read the second time and the House went into Committee thereon, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.
On section 2-schqpl lands may be dealt with as other lands in irrigation district.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The object of the Bill is simply this. In 1916 we passed a Bill to enable certain school lands to be included in an irrigation district, but we did not provide that the district debentures should be a first charge on these lands but only a charge subject to the claim of the Dominion Government in the case of lands sold. Under these conditions it became impossible to organize the district and proceed with the work.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I understand that a syndicate owned these lands in the West, but being unable to go on with the work within the time specified in the letters patent, the Government granted an extension of time and even made certain advances to the company. Is not that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I do not know that the hon. member has the syndicate idea right. Irrigation districts are formed under provincial legislation. They are, of course, in the nature of a syndicate. They were unable to carry on this enterprise because they could not use the school lands in the same way as the other lands under the provincial legislation, and issue debentures making a first charge against the school lands. I communicated with the Government of the province, and it is their desire that the school lands, in which they are interested as beneficiaries, should be placed in the same position as the other lands, so that debentures wrill form the same charge

upon them that they form upon private lands. That is the purpose of the Bill.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I would point out that the school lands are actually being benefited by this legislation. In these particular districts where the school lands are left under what we may call "dry" conditions they are of little value, but once they are placed under irrigation their value is increased, I might say, a hundredfold. We have irrigation around the city of Lethbridge, and sales of irrigated land take place there frequently at from $135 to $150 an acre, whereas $40 would be a very high price for what is commonly known as "dry" land. These irrigation districts have been created by the provinces and are somewhat similar to municipalities. They are given certain powers, and it is necessary that these school lands be treated the same as the other lands in the district in order that the irrigation project may be proceeded with. My argument is that it will be of benefit to the school lands to be included in this irrigated district, because it will increase their value; they will be more easy to cultivate, be more productive, and more worth while to the School Lands Fund.
Mr. LEMIEUX; This Bill applies to only one district?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Yes, the Taber Irrigation District.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Why do you not make the law general?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: We could not do so without the consent of the provinces affected, and I do not think the provinces would be ready to consent to. general legislation that would enable us to create a charge on any locality we chose. That would put it out of the power of the province to retain their beneficial interest in any school lands whatever. Before we charge any special set of school lands on the ground that they are going to be benefited by being brought into an irrigation district, I think the province would want to exercise some supervision as to what lands should be so included.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: At all events we are creating a precedent, and if later on any one else applies for the application of the same principle the Government will give them the same privilege.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
If the Government's irrigation officers are of the opinion that it is irrigable land, that the project is feasible,
and if the province agrees; I see no other conditions which should be imposed.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: This Bill is a little difficult to understand. It refers to an Act passed by the legislature of Alberta, which Act we have not before us. Will this involve any expenditure on the part of the Government?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: No. Otherwise I would have had to bring down a resolution to precede the Bill. The only expenditure by the Government in work of this kind is for survey purposes.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Out of the general
fund?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Our responsibility ends with the survey work, that is, investigating the feasibility of the project.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Is the object of the Bill this, that if this irrigation company improves any lands that are set aside for school purposes the debentures shall be a lien on these school lands?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: That is the object exactly.	,

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 5-statutes of 1916, c. 26 repealed.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: WThat is the meaning of this?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: That is the statute I referred to which enabled this to be done, but did not enable a first charge to be created.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: By what authority will the debentures be issued?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The Provincial Government of Alberta.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I spoke of a syndicate. The minister has spoken of a private company.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
There is no private
company and no syndicate. It is the province that creates an irrigation district by general statute. It is formed as a drainage district is formed. These districts have certain corporate powers and issue bonds chargeable, according to certain principles, upon land affected, in proportion, to the benefit accrued.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Bill reported, read the third time and passed.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I should like to be able this afternoon to take up the resolution

concerning judges' salaries, and after that the amendment to the Dominion Lands Act; but I see that although this latter measure was introduced some days ago it has not yet been printed.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Is it printed in French?
Mr. MEIOH1EN: I do not even see the English copy. It is anything at all but an important measure, for the reason that it has already been preceded by resolution, carried some time ago, but I did not then go on with the Bill.
Mr. LEMIE'UX: Could you not get it for this afternoon?

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: Motion agreed to, and the House went into Committee, Mr. Boivin in the Chair.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, by
these resolutions it is proposed to increase the salaries of all the county court judges in all the provinces except the province of Quebec. It is also proposed to increase by $1,000 the salaries of the judge of the high courts of the western provinces as well as those of the Maritime Provinces, in order that they may be put on the same level as the salaries of judges of equal rank in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. There is absolutely nothing proposed with regard to the salaries of the judges of the province of Quebec. If the Bill which is to be introduced has for its purpose to equalize the salaries of judges of the same jurisdiction and having the same rank, there are, I believe, fifteen judges of the High Court of Quebec whose salaries should be increased to bring them up to the level of the salaries of twenty-seven other judges of that province having the same jurisdiction and belonging to the same court. There is an anomaly existing in the province in that regard. There are twenty-one judges of the Superior Court appointed for the district of Montreal; those judges have a salary of $7,000 each. There are six other judges appointed for the district of Quebec, and they have the same salary. It is proposed that the judges of the Superior Courts of all the provinces shall have the same salaries, and it will be seen that these twenty-seven judges of the province of Quebec are already getting the maximum. But what about the fifteen other judges of the province who have only a $5,000 salary? There are, for instance, two judges for the district of Three Rivers and Nicolet. They are judges of the High Court and have the same rank and jurisdiction as the judges of the Superior Court of Montreal and Quebec. As a matter of fact, I believe they have more work to do than the judges who preside in the cities of Montreal and Quebec; but they are placed in an inferior position in regard to salary. The same thing may be said of the judges of the district of Sherbrooke. There are two judges sitting in that very important district, and they are also in an inferior position as far as salary is concerned, their salary being only $5,000. The same thing applies to the judges of the districts of Arthabaska, Bedford, Iberville, Joliette, Kamouraska, Pontiac and Rimouski; all those judges have salaries of only $5,000. Why not apply to these fifteen judges the same principle of equalization of salaries which is to be applied to the
judges of the High Courts of all the provinces of the Dominion? I claim in all fairness that those fifteen judges should be put on the same level as all the judges of the High Courts of all the provinces of the Dominion. There is an exception in the case of the judges of Prince Edward Island, who are left in an inferior position; and I believe that this should also be redressed and that the three judges of the High Court of that province should have equal salaries with the other High Court judges of the Dominion.
Now, to illustrate how unfair it is, I will quote the case of a judge of the province of Quebec. In 1914, owing to the surplus of judicial work in the city of Montreal, and the many complaints made by the bar and the bench of the city, the legislature-because the administration of justice and the organization of tribunals belongs to the provinces according to the constitution-made an amendment to the law, providing that the judge of the districts of Beauharnois, Richelieu, St. Hya-cinthe and Pontiac should reside thereafter in the city of Montreal and should sit in the city for the judicial affairs of the district of Montreal while not engaged in their own districts. At the following session an amendment was made to the Judges' Act, placing three of those judges on the same level, as far as salary is concerned, as the other judges of the district of Montreal, and those whose residence was thereafter fixed in the city of Montreal were granted an additional sum of $2,000. One exception was made in the case of the judge of Pontiac district (Mr. Justice Weir). Although he is also obliged now to live in Montreal and to work in the district, he was not placed in the same position, and is only entitled to a salary of $5,000. I noticed that anomaly and I inquired the reasons for such a discrimination. Although Mr. Justice Weir has had to live in Montreal since that law was passed, and is attending to his judicial duties in the city and district of Montreal, he is placed in a position of inferiority.
Certain correspondence was exchanged between the Attorney General of the province of Quebec and the Department of Justice, of which I happened to take cognizance, and I noticed that the Minister of Justice always refused to accept the amendments which had been passed by the Legislature of Quebec as far as the district of Pontiac is concerned, and always refused to grant to the judge of Pontiac district the increase which had been granted to other

judges placed in the same position. That shows the discrimination and unfairness in having judges of the same rank, and of the same court, and exercising the same jurisdiction, placed in a position of inequality. It is a discrimination that tells against those judges, and I do not think it is fair for this Parliament to create such discrimination. Not only should the judge of the district of Pontiac be given a salary of $7,000 like the other judges of the district of Montreal, but that salary should also be given to all the fifteen judges of the Superior Court of Quebec who now receive only $5,000 when the other twenty-seven judges of the province of Quebec receive $7,000, which salary will also be given hereafter to the judges in all the other provinces.
Mr. McISAA'C: If my hon. friend (Air. Ernest Lapointe) has occasion for exception regarding the inequality of judges' salaries in the province of Quebec, I, speaking on behalf of the province of Prince Edward Island, have much greater reason for complaint. Prior to the introduction of this resolution a very great discrepancy and inequality existed between the salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island and the salaries of like judges in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and in other provinces as well. Confining ourselves, however, to the Maritime Provinces: The Chief Justices in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia received $7,000 and the puisne judges in the same provinces, of courts of like jurisdiction, $6,000. On the other hand, the Chief Justice of Prince Edward Island received $6,000 and each of the puisne judges, or, as they are called, assistant judges-one being the Master of the Rolls and the other Vice Chancellor-received a salary of $5,200. Under the re-adjustment it was expected that this inequality would be removed. Why should there be any difference between the salaries of judges in Prince Edward Island and the salaries of judges of similar courts elsewhere? I must believe that it requires as much of ability, of devotion to duty, and of every other quality that constitutes a competent judge to fill the position of Judge of the Supreme Court of Prince Edward Island, as in the case of judges in the courts of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick-or any other province, for that matter-particularly when it is borne in mind that in Prince Edward Island three judges do the work which is performed by seven or eight judges in these other provinces. And so far as the cost of living is concerned, it is just as expensive to live in

Prince Edward Island nowadays as anywhere else in Canada. If we take all these reasons into consideration I cannot understand why the existing inequality is not only perpetuated, but accentuated and aggravated under the proposed legislation. Now, what does the Government propose to do under these resolutions? It proposes to advance the salaries of the chief justices in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia from $7,000 ,to $8,000 and the salaries of the puisne judges of the respective courts in these provinces from $6,000 to $7,000. In Prince Edward Island the salary of the chief justice is to be advanced from $6,000 to $6,500, creating an inequality between his salary and the salary of the judges of corresponding courts in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia of $1,500; that is to say the existing difference is increased from $500 to $1,500. That is something I can scarcely understand. And in the case oi the assistant judges of Prince Edward Island, the increase only amounts to $300. This, I repeat, not only continues the discrimination and inequality between the salaries of the Prince Edward Island judges and the salaries of like judges in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and all the other provinces, but even renders it much more marked. I am at a loss to understand why it is, if adjustments were to be undertaken and the salaries of judges were to be equalized, as we expected, that, so far as the province from which I come is concerned, tlm inequality, discrepancy, and injustice which formerly prevailed, as compared with the judges of the other provinces has been increased to the extent of from $1,000 and $800 respectively, to $1,500. The salaries of our judges are not only not relatively improved as compared with the judges in other provinces, but are left in a much worse condition comparatively than they were before. For these reasons, I would like the Acting Minister of Justice to explain -why this very great inequality and injustice is perpetuated and aggravated as regards the judges of Prince Edward Island.

speechtext: I desire to say, Mr. Chairman-

speechtext: The hon. member for Three Rivers (Air. Bureau) has the floor.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I will give way to the Acting Minister of Justice if he desires to speak, because I wish to hear his explanation first.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
When I see so many hon. members desiring to rise, and being

apprehensive that each of them is opposed to some feature of the Bill, I begin to think that I was not altogether unwise in endeavouring to shelve this measure until the return of the Minister of Justice himself. I have no anticipation that any possible rearrangement of judicial salaries could be proposed to the House which would be acceptable all around.
The hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. E. Lapointe) referred to the Bench of the province of Quebec, and contends that they are not fairly dealt with by this measure as compared with the judges of the other provinces; and the hon. member for King's (Mr. Mclsaac), complains in a similar strain of the salaries paid to the Bench in Prince Edward Island. The province of Quebec has a distribution of judicial jurisdiction that differs from all the other provinces of Canada. The courts to which my hon. friend (Mr. Ernest Lapointe) has referred are manned by judges in Quebec and Montreal, twenty-seven in all, with salaries of $7,000 each, the Chief Justice in each case getting $8,000, and in that respect they are just the same as the judges in the province of Ontario. The other judges in the Superior Court exercising the same functions as county court and district judges in the other provinces receive $5,000. There is no court in the province of Quebec corresponding with what is known as the county court in Western Canada and the district court in other portions of the Dominion. The work done by county and district court judges elsewhere is taken care of in Quebec by judges who exercise, as well, a somewhat higher jurisdiction, dealing, I believe, with larger amounts of money. That being the ease it is impossible to have any measure than can be said to yield salaries to judges in the other provinces absolutely equal to those paid in Quebec. In the province of Quebec there are twenty-seven judges, according to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Lapointe), who draw $7,000 a year. That is not the case in any other province in Canada. The number who draw those higher salaries is much more limited even in the province of Ontario. Then there are a number of judges who are drawing $5,000, whereas there are none who perform similar duties drawing salaries as high in any other province of Canada. Our own judges in the province of Manitoba will draw less, very materially less, even under the present measure. In this connection let me say that very strong pressure has been brought to bear to have those salaries
raised and, as well, the salaries of the higher judges in the province of Ontario.
Delegations On behalf of the higher Bench of Ontario have waited upon the Government and urged in the strongest possible terms that the salaries of the judges of these higher courts be increased so that they shall be on a level with those in the province of Quebec. They claimed that by virtue of a different nomenclature the salaries in the province of Quebec were higher in the aggregate than they were in Ontario.
I did not share in that view; it seemed to me that there was not a very great difference in that regard. But it would have been impossible to raise the level of the salaries of the judges in these courts in Quebec without also making some changes in the salaries of judges of the higher courts of Ontario.
Then there was the question whether the salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada, having regard to the status of that court and to its very great importance, were not inconsistent with the dignity of that court and the ability of the men who must have seats therein. But having regard to the fact that the primary cause of the action now being taken is the increase in the cost of living and in the necessity of enabling those whose salaries were on the lower salary scale to maintain themselves and their families as they should be maintained, I thought that my best course was to increase the salaries of those who were on the lower scale, and not to touch those on the higher scale, who, though not drawing what they did draw in former years, having regard to the 'increased cost of living, still were drawing sufficient to enable them to live in fair comfort. So I decided not to recommend any change in the salaries of the judges in the higher courts of Canada. But that remark should be qualified by one exception. The salaries of the judges of the higher courts in the western provinces and in the Maritime Provinces had never been on a level with those of judges in similar courts in Ontario and Quebec. Every year since I first came to Parliament it has been urged upon me most strongly that an undue discrimination existed there, that it should never have existed, and that it should be wiped away. I never felt that the argument was wholly sound. In the earlier and smaller stages of the commercial and population development of these provinces there was some reason for not placing the judges of their higher courts on a level, as to
