speechtext: How many district, and county court judges have we in Canada, or how many will there be under this arrangement?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I will give them province by province: Ontario has 75 county court judges; a reduction of 25, I believe, is specifically provided for, and the Lieutenant Governor in Council, if I understand the legislation aright, has power thereafter to reduce the number of judges by the amalgamation of districts. So the bench in Ontario will be very substantially reduced. Nova Scotia has 7 county court judges, New Brunswick 6, Manitoba 9, British Columbia 14, Prince Edward Island 3, Saskatchewan 18, and Alberta 12. The Yukon has one judge, whose salary is $5,000, and who draws as well a living allowance of $5,000. I have not felt there was any necessity for increasing the salary of the judge in the Yukon Territory.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I want to lay my case before the committee, and I am going to request the Acting Minister of Justice, before I am through, to re-consider these resolutions and grant the request made by my hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe), that the Superior Court judges in the province ot Quebec be put on an even footing. The minister has stated that there must have *been reasons for this difference in salary when the salaries were apportioned. The only surmise I can make, and it seems to me reasonable, is that there must have been one of two reasons for the difference in salaries; first, that the work in certain districts was not as considerable as in others, or second, that the cost of living was higher in the cities than in the country. As to qualifications, it makes no difference whether the judge presides over a population of 90,000 people or 14,000 people; the responsibility is no greater. The minister has given us the number of the county court judges in the different provinces. Quebec was not in that list because it has no county court judges. The only judges of limited jurisdiction in the province of Quebec are four in number, I believe-the exact number I do not know, because I do not practise in their district, but they have jurisdiction to the amount of $200. They are located in the city of Montreal, and their jurisdiction is coextensive with the limits of the district of Montreal. The judges of the Superior Court in the province of Quebec have unlimited jurisdiction, absolutely unlimited, extending from a penny to any amount that the imagination can conceive. Some of

these judges who lived, at the time our judiciary was established, in the cities of Montreal and Quebec, are getting $7,000.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: What about Three Rivers?

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
The judge of the district of Three Rivers is getting only $5,000. Other judges, including the districts of St. Hyacinthe, Richelieu, and I think Beau-harnois, all of which are rural districts, feceive $7,000, because their residence is established in Montreal and they help the Montreal judges. If salary is based upon the responsibility and the amount of work done by a judge, I say that the judge of the district of Three Rivers-seeing that that district has been mentioned-ought to receive $9,000, as against $7,000 in other cases, and I will tell you why. If the salary is based on the cost of living, let me say at once that there is absolutely no difference between the expenditure incurred by the man who lives in the city I have the honour to come from, and the man who lives in Montreal or Quebec, in respect of fuel, taxes and everything else. As far as the necessities of life are concerned, they are higher in city of Three Rivers than in Montreal. We have no big departmental stores such as they have in Montreal, and no bargain sales. For these reasons it costs more to live in the city of Three Rivers than it does in Montreal. Kow, as to the work. In the cities of Montreal and Quebec a judge of the Court of the King's Bench presides over the criminal assizes. In the district of Three Rivers the Court of King's Bench during criminal assizes is presided over by a judge of the Superior Court, and the same is true of all the other rural judicial districts. Furthermore, in the city of Montreal you have four judges of the Circuit Court who have jurisdiction to the amount of $200, but you have none in the rural districts nor in the city of Quebec either, and consequently the judge of the Superior Court sits in the circuit court over cases coming before that court. He also sits in review. Under our judicial system our first appeal is to a court of review, composed of three judges chosen by the chief justice from among the judges of the superior court. I am not going to say whether the court of review ought to remain or disappear. The point I am making is that the judge of the superior court also presides at the assizes and sits as a member of the court of review. Then, in all cases under the municipal code, if you are not satisfied with

your assessment, and so forth, the appeal lies to the judge of the superior court sitting as a judge of appeal with final jurisdiction. Under the Cities and Towns Act, and under the municipal code, if you have a controverted election case it comes before the judge of the superior court sitting as a judge, in certain cases, of the circuit court.
Our railway expropriation law has been changed, and mostly all, and I dare say all expropriations are made under the provisions of the Provincial Kailway Act and under this Act, for the last two, if not three years, the judge of the superior court sits as an arbitrator; that is, instead of having two arbitrators, one appointed by either side, and the third agreed upon by those two or appointed by the judge, the judge of the superior court sits as an arbitrator and hears all expropriation cases. He sits also as a court of appeal in all cases having reference to the infringement of fish and game laws.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
And election protest
cases.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Yes, of course. Then in connection with the Employers' Liability Act in certain provinces, cases brought under that Act are heard by a board, in our province, instead of having a board of arbitration, you cannot bring an action unless you petition the court, and that petition is granted de jure. There is a provision that when the petition is laid before the court the parties can come together, and although not a regular proceeding with summons and all the requirements of the code of civil procedure, in order to avoid costs and help the employee the judge has the right after hearing them to confirm the arrangement by a judgment which is binding on the parties. Under our Compensation Act any agreement made between the parties themselves is declared null and void. Those are the duties which our judges have to perform.
May I say that at the time the judge was appointed to the district of Three Rivers, I think the population of the city did not exceed 4,000 or 5,000, and outside of Three Rivers there was absolutely nothing. The only industry in the city of Three Rivers then was a small sawmill, which we used to call the American sawmill. Peace reigned among the farmers. In those days the word of a man was worth something; when he gave his word he kept it, and written contracts,. notes and receipts signed and witnessed were not as much in vogue as they are to-day, because they were not as necessary as they are today. So you can well imagine the litigation then could not compare in amount with the litigation of to-day. The city of Three Rivers has grown from 4,000 or 5,000 people until to-day it has a population of 25,000. Besides the sawmill I have mentioned we have three big pulp mills and two shipyards. Not a day passes but two or three cases come before our courts under one law alone. You can easily understand that with the
10,000	or 12,000 men employed in steel and wooden shipbuilding and in our paper mills, accidents are common. A Superior Court judge tries all these accident cases. Within the district of Three Rivers, twenty miles north of that city, is Shawinigan Falls with a population of 15,000 people, of whom I should say from 8,000 to 10,000 people work in industrial enterprises. Among other things we make chemicals at Shawinigan Falls. We have located there the Chemical Electro-Products Company, with a plant * costing over $2,000,000, and accidents there are very, very frequent. I do not know if hon. gentlemen are familiar with the process of manufacturing aluminum. We manufacture that article at Shawinigan Falls.
The things that are manufactured there require a great amount of power, which can be got reasonably cheap. Nature has helped considerably to make conditions favourable. The men who work there are exposed to great perils. They work in intense heat and are surrounded by wires and electrodes and accidents happen every day. Another industry which is carried on there and which is fraught with danger is the manufacture of calcium carbide. I believe it is also made in St. Catharines, and in this industry accidents happen very frequently. I do not think I exaggerate when I say that in this one industry alone there is one accident a week. Now here is one judge who has to hear all these petitions. You cannot go before the court unless you make a petition, and it has to be heard and passed upon by him. The law says that the petition shall be granted unless the parties come to an agreement or unless it is evident, on the face of the petition, that the judge has no jurisdiction or that the case does not come within the compensation Act. But whether he refuses to grant it or not, he has to hear the petition. The judge at Three Rivers has a vast volume of work to perform. My hon. friend (Mr. E. Lapointe) calls my attention to the Laurentide Pulp and .Paper company, which is quite well known, and which does a considerable amount of work in Grand'Mere.

There is a rural population of over 100,000 people. At Grand'Mere there is the Laurentide Paper company, a very large concern. It is just as well to mention these facts to show what the judge at Three Rivers has to do. There is at La Tuque an important corporation, the Brown Corporation, manufacturing 200 tons of pulp a day, and necessarily numerous accidents occur. Besides that we have large lumber mills, and forestry operations, and under our jurisprudence cases of men who are drowned or receive injuries in various logging operations come under this Act. Now, is it right that because fifty years ago the town of Three Rivers had a population of only
3,000	or 4,000, with nothing but fields surrounding it, a position that was then worth $5,000 should remain at that figure now? In Montreal and Quebec the law societies have large and well-equipped libraries, and the universities of Laval and McGill being located in Quebec and Montreal, more young men go from those cities to the universities to read law than do men from Three Rivers. The fees that have to he paid by students either to be admitted to Tead law or to be admitted to the bar are paid largely in Montreal and Quebec, and practically all young men- go there; at any rate, the number in our district and all other rural districts is so small that we cannot keep an adequate library. Most of the lawyers in our district, and the judge have to buy their own books, and I need only appeal to my confreres in this House who will appreciate the cost. . All the reports must be kept up and subscriptions paid. In Montreal there are twenty-one judges, and if one judge has a case which is difficult or which embarrasses him he consults with his fellow-judges, talks the matter over with them and receives the benefit of their opinions. On the other hand, the man who is alone has more work to do than any of those judges because he has to hunt things up for himself and has to look up every point of law without the assistance of the opinions of other judges. He is absolutely dependent upon himself and has not the assistance in the way of collaboration which the judges in the larger places enjoy. In this way it is obvious that he has greater responsibilities. Take a new district like the St. Maurice valley which, barring British Columbia-because they have high mountains-is one of the best water-power valleys in Canada. The powers developed on the St. Maurice are better than in any of the provinces this side of the Rocky Mountains. Before electricity came general-
ly into use the people did not attach much importance either to the water-powers or to the banks of rivers or the lands adjacent. But the moment the use of electricity spread and became popular these lands increased in value, and what happened in the West happened in the region of the St. Maurice valley. Before the increase in value it was easy to make an arrangement with the farmer who was the riparian owner, if development operations were contemplated. But with the advent of higher prices it became necessary to expropriate because bazaar prices were demanded and the power holders were not willing to accept low terms. The judge of the Superior Court receiving $5,000 had, and still has, to sit day after day to hear those expropriation cases. Although it may be a matter for disagreement, our legislature at all events found that it was cheaper and better, instead of having three arbitrators possessing no knowledge [DOT]of the rules of evidence, and their wrangling for three days over a case, to have the judge of the Superior Court act as arbitrator.
Now, these are the conditions, and I submit that it is only fair that this resolution should be amended so as to put all judges of the Superior Court who have equal jurisdiction and responsibility and who must have equal education and ability and legal acumen, on the same footing.	The reason given by my hon.
friend for this not being done is the absence of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Doherty). The province of Quebec, I might say, is unrepresented in the Cabinet-especially in important cases such as this-except by the Minister of Justice. Through no instrumentality of the province of the province of Quebec, has the Minister of Justice, been chosen to go across the seas to sign the Treaty of Peace. Well, it is a great honour and the province of Quebec must be flattered. But because the Minister of Justice is absent, is that any reason why all the other provinces which have not the honour of being represented by a Minister or Justice, are roing to be taken into consideration, while the province of Quebec-which, I must say, has the misfortune this time to have the Minister of Justice coming from its own midst-is ignored? This injustice will continue. My hon. friend said just now that there was no discrimination, but this is discrimination of the worst kind. Indeed, it is not only discrimination but injustice. I will not take the excuse of my hou. friend the Acting Minister of Justice. We did not appoint the Minister of Justice ourselves, and I do not see why there might

to be any discrimination because the Minister of Justice comes from the province of Quebec. If my hon. friend went to the judges of the rural districts and asked them if they were willing to resign the honour of having the Minister of Justice come from Quebec or, on the other hand, take the
82,000	more, there would be no hesitation in their decision. It is altogether a flimsy excuse to say that the Minister of Justice hails from Quebec and happens to be absent rendering service to his country, and that therefore Quebec should be ignored. Now we say that the circumstances have ceased which existed when these salaries were' determined, and we want you now to consider conditions as they are and to equalize these salaries. Therefore I -would ask my hon. friend if he would take that resolution back to Council, and I am satisfied that after hearing just one part of the case, as it ought to be submitted-because I know I forget a great many things in enumerating the work of these judges, and I also forget a good many things that I should say in regard to the increased cost of living, which exists in the smaller towns as it does in the larger-I repeat, I am satisfied that under these circumstances Council will recognize that it is only just and fair that this resolution should be reconsidered and the judges of the Superior Courts of the province of Quebec put on the same footing as other judges of similar rank. I do not want the members of this committee to forget that we have no county judges other than the judges of the Superior Courts, and they have absolutely unlimited jurisdiction.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: * Mr, Chairman, I wish to register my protest against this legislation for the reasons adduced by my hon. friend from Three Rivers and Kamouraska. I do not begrudge any increase of salary to the judges of the other provinces, but I say that my hon. friend (Mr. Meighen) and the Government should have dealt with the judges of the province of Quebec in the same way as they have dealt with the judges of the other provinces. The judicial system of the province of Quebec has been well described by my hon. friend from Three Rivers. We have no seventy-two county court judges as they have in the province of Ontario. We have district magistrates, who have similar jurisdiction to that of the county court judges of Ontario, but they are not paid by the Federal Government-I wish to draw this distinction at once.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: What jurisdiction have they?

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: They have criminal and civil jurisdiction.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: What civil jurisdiction? Mr. E. LAPOINTE: Up to $50, as a rule.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Up to $90, I think. At all events they have criminal and civil jurisdiction.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Are they magistrates or judges? In Ontario our county court judges have jurisdiction in actions for libel, slander, and all that sort of thing.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I am not speaking of
the ordinary justices of the peace. I am speaking of district magistrates having a jurisdiction covering a large territory and sitting in criminal cases; they have also civil jurisdiction, and they are very busy men. I am not referring now to the police magistrates of the city of Montreal or of the city of Quebec, but I am speaking of the district magistrates as they have them in the districts of the province, and they are paid out of the provincial treasury. As to judges of the Superior Court, as my hon. friend from Three Rivers said a moment ago, they have unlimited jurisdiction. At the time of Confederation,' when the judicial system was organized, it was thought that it would be to the advantage of the people that the judges should reside in their districts. At that time there was no railway communication except by the Grand Trunk, but since then there has been such a multiplication of railway facilities in our province, as everywhere else, that that consideration does not stand; and, besides, it has been felt in the rural districts that there should be an interchange of judges, because the same judge always administering justice with the same lawyers is apt at times to be the unwilling source of injustice. Since the railway systems have been extended the city of Montreal especially, and also the cities of Three Rivers and Quebec, have expanded so much that the business requirements make it incumbent on the chief justice to call on the judges of the rural districts to help in those cities. I remember when a boy that the population of Montreal did not reach 200,000; now it is 700,000. These district judges are men, generally speaking, who enjoyed a very high reputation in the practice of their profession before being elevated to the bench, and they have more to do than the judges of the Superior



Courts in Montreal or Quebec, for they have to preside over the criminal courts at every term, and in addition to that they have to sit as judges of the circuit courts. I have here some figures for the year 1917 of the number of writs issued in five of the districts. In the circuit court of the district of Arthabaska 963 writs were issued; in Beauce, 1,008; .in Joliette, 737; in St. Hyacinthe, 2,200; in Three Rivers, where they have two judges, 1,726; and judgments were rendered in all these cases. In the Superior Courts for the same year the number of writs issued were as follows:- for the district of Arthabaska, 393; Beauce, 452; Chicoutimi, 274; St. Hyacinthe, 699; Three Rivers, 738. Those judges are also called upon to sit in the Court of Review in Montreal. There is no reason why they should not be treated on a footing of equality with the judges of the city of Montreal or the city of Quebec.
For many years an agitation has gone on, the bar has taken up the question and from the various districts resolutions have been passed and sent to the Minister of Justice, praying the Government to treat those judges as they do the judges of Montreal and Quebec. Why should there be any discrimination? I am sorry that my hon. friend has ignored the demands of the resolutions forwarded to the Department of Justice, and I sincerely hope that he will reconsider his decision; because while we do not object to the judges in the other provinces receiving a fair salary as judges, we think that the judges in our province should be dealt with on the same principle. I am confident that if the Minister of Justice had been here, knowing the situation as he does, he would certainly have treated the judges of his own province more liberally than my hon. friend does in this Bill. I do not say that he does it out of any animus against the province of Quebec, not at all.
But it seems strange, when this Bill is being introduced in order to equalize the salaries of the judges in the other provinces with those of the judges in the province of Quebec, that in our province there should still remain an inequality between the salaries paid to the judges in rural districts and the salaries paid to the judges in Montr real and Quebec, and as to which we have been asking the Government for years to carry out an equalization.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I am of the opinion that in the province of Ontario, even after this legislation passes, there will still be some inequality between the salaries paid to 
judges in cities and the salaries paid to judges in the rural districts. As to that I am not sure. I know there has always been such an inequality, but it may have been abolished in that province. But what the hon. gentleman (iMr. Lemieux) does not impress upon the House is this: He says that in order to have equality you must raise the salaries of the rural judges of the Superior Court in Quebec to $7,000, the amount which is paid to judges in Quebec and Montreal. But that would mean that we should have in Quebec forty-two judges each enjoying a salary of $7,000, and I doubt whether we have one-half of that number of seven thousand-dollar judges even in Ontario. The hon. gentleman must remember this. It may be, I believe it is, that the magistrates in the province of Quebec, who are provincially appointed, have certain jurisdiction in civil cases. Well, that is the case in other provinces as well; the magistrates have jurisdiction in civil cases of certain kinds, although not in all civil cases, in the other provinces; it may be, however, Jhat the magistrates provincially appointed have a somewhat wider jurisdiction in Quebec than in any other province of Canada. But it is also true that the province of Quebec does not provide for the trial of smaller civil cases, and less important quasi-criminal cases, by judges of a lower standing and lower pay, as in the other provinces.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: We do; there are justices of the peace.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
But they have only
jurisdiction up to a most limited figure, up to $50. Whether in all the provinces justices of the peace can determine cases I am not sure, but in some provinces the jurisdiction extends up to $100 if the cases arise from certain causes which embrace most of those cases tried. It may be that the justices of the peace in Quebec try civil cases of greater importance than do justices of the peace in other provinces.
What I say, and I want to impress the fact upon the House, is that the province of Quebec does not provide for the trial of these smaller civil cases by a lower rank of judges, lower paid, as do all the other provinces of Confederation. For example, if a case arises in that province involving $75, as pointed out by hon. members who have spoken, that $75 case must be tried by a judge who is paid $7,000, if it is in the city of Montreal or the city of Quebec.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Oh, no. The hon. gentleman. will pardon me, but there are four circuit judges in Montreal who try those cases.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: What salary do they draw?

speechtext:
No doubt if the province of Quebec had constituted courts analogous to the courts of the other provinces the salaries would have been the same; but under present circumstances if you are going to raise the salaries <^f the judges in Quebec to the maximum amount paid you are going to have a tremendously high-paid Bench in that province compared with that of the other provinces. That appears to have been recognized always, even when the Minister of Justice was from that province and from the same ranks as hon. gentlemen opposite. The same recognition is continued here, the same difference of salary. But the very same arguments that have been urged by hon. gentlemen opposite were urged all during those years. It may be that the arguments now have somewhat stronger force .as applied to the city of Three Rivers and to other points. I would not say they have not force to warrant an increase in such cases, but I do say that in respect of individual cases of the kind they would be better taken care of later when the Minister of Justice returns to the country. They would be better understood by the minister himself; and the whole local situation can be better understood by him, because, after all, it is now more a matter of domestic arrangement than anything else and of the appreciation of the relative responsibilities of individual judges. Therefore the Bill as it stands should not wait until such subjects as that can be taken into account.
I wish further to call the attention of the House to some observations that the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs) made during a recent debate in connection with this question, his remarks having to do with inattention to duty on the part of certain members of the Bench of the city of Montreal. Those re-268i
marks were brought to the attention of" the Chief Justice of the province who took very serious objection thereto and wrote me the following letter which I think I should read in justice to the Bench of the.' city of Montreal:
Montreal, June 10, 1919. Dear Sir,-In the7 Hansard for the 30th May, on page 3064, reporting a speech by Mr. Jacobs, I find the following:-
"Within the last few years there have been made to the Bench appointments of five men, who probably consider that they have been placed there simply as pensioners, because little is ever done by these gentlemen to see that speedy judgments are handed down. I speak about this matter advisedly, and while probably I am somewhat out of order, I hope that bringing this matter to the attention of the committee will make some of these judges understand that they are after all servants of the public as other people in the civil service are, and that they must do their duty as other employees in the Government service do."
The whole effect of IMr. Jacobs' speech was to convey the impression that the Judges in the Province of Quebec were idle, negligent, and careless, either of the duty or dignity of their profession.	[DOT]
Having in charge the administration of justice in the western end of the province, X repel with indignation the charges of Mr. Jacobs; but I am better acquainted of course, with the state of things in the district of Montreal, and I can say that there is only one of the twenty-one judges, who reside and perform their functions in Montreal, who has any case which has been before him en d41ib6r6 more than six months.
The one exception has a few cases beyond a year, but that has been caused by his serious illness. I am personally aware that he has worked up to and even beyond his strength and is still continuing to do so, even against the advice of his medical adviser.
It is, I think, very unfortunate that a member of Parliament, and especially a member of the iBar, should deem himself justified in making charges of the character of those which Mr. Jacobs has made in the House of Commons and under cover of Parliamentary privilege.
I hope you will see your way to notice this matter officially.
I am, yours very truly,
J. F. Archibald.

speechtext: I want to say a word or two in support of what has been already said in regard to this legislation and against the discrimination that exists in the schedule of salaries contained therein as respects the judges of the province of Prince Edward Island from which I have the honour to come. I wish to deal with the matter from two standpoints. First, let me say that the discrimination in question has always existed in the salaries paid to the judges in Prince Edward Island as compared with the salaries paid: to the judges in other provinces. The minister has told us that this discrimination has

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I have so often tried in this House to get something for the men in the country's service who are lamentably underpaid-men who get from $600 to $1,000 a year-that I find myself in a new atmosphere when I have to get up and support a proposal to increase the salaries of those who are in higher positions and getting more money. I was veTy much impressed by the argument of my hon. friend (Mr. Bureau) with reference to the work done by the judges in the district of which he spoke. I am under the impression that the country is following a wrong principle in the matter of the application, of remuneration in such cases as this. A judge should be paid for the work that he does. The remuneration for all County Court judges in Ontario is $3,000, with the possible exception of judges in Hamilton, Toronto, Ottawa, and London; though I am not sure that the exception applies now in all these cases. Ontario, therefore, recognizes the principle that I now advocate, the principle that in the larger centres, where there is more work to be done, the judges should get larger remuneration than is paid in the smaller centres where there is less work.
In Ontario there are many judges who are not overworked, who, really, in many counties, have not. enough to keep them going nicely, and yet they must perform the service to the State from one'year's end to the other, and be at their post to adjudicate upon the business that the community sends in to the court for them to preside over. My idea is that there should be a
standardization below which no judge-should be asked to perform his functions. Let that standardization, if you like, be $4,000 as is proposed now-and by the way I do not exactly see why all of the district judges in Quebec should ge't $5,000 remuneration, with the salaries of Ontario judges in past years standing at $3,000. I know many Ontario judges, outside of the cities of Toronto, Ottawa, Hamilton and London, who are very hard-worked and are entitled to more money, but the principle that should be followed is the standardization of judges' salaries at such a sum-and a moderate sum-as will enable them to live properly having regard to the position they occupy in the community.. Beyond that, where in a county there is thrown upon a judge an excessive amount of work-and many counties that I know of furnish such cases-that judge should be paid a reasonable advance over the standard salary commensurate with the business that is sent to him. I appreciate the difficulty of arriving at that, but I believe the returns in the hands of the Provincial Government, showing the number-of writs issued, the number of cases that: come actually to trial and the disposition of them, the criminal work the county court judges have to do, would enable the Government to estimate very fairly and to fix a remuneration for those counties. There are in Ontario certain counties that are known as non-litigous counties; there are others, perhaps including a town of ten or fifteen thousand people, with diversified interests-although in a different style from that referred to by the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau),-which produce all kinds of litigation. A county here will have a busy judge, and there right next to it will be a county with, I would not like to say an idle judge, but a judge who is not very busy. A man should be-paid for the work he does; and while I do. not oppose this Bill, it would be worth while taking into consideration for the-future some other principle than that of an absolutely universal increase all along the line. I should like to call the attention of the Acting Minister of Justice (Mr. Meighen) to the fact that the Ontario Government have decided to do away as far as possible with the principle of having two judges in a county, and that is going to throw~ more work upon the judge who remains. Therefore, as I see it to-day in Ontario the Government is going to win on that principle and save a good deal of salary.

speechtext:
There is not very much difference between them and the county' court judges of Ontario because the jurisdiction of the Ontario county court judge, except, say, in case of libel and slander in which the verdict is limited to a maximum of $500, has been extended, and in all actions, commercial and criminal, the county court judge of Ontario is frequently a busier man than many Supreme Court judges, and I venture to say, just as busy as some of the Quebec judges who are drawing the extra $1,000. Therefore, if the salaries of such Ontario county court judges were to be put on the same basis as others, I do not see what hon. members opposite from Quebec have to complain about. The Ontario judges have a great deal to complain about in the fact that the minister, by the proposed Bill, is raising their stipend *only by $1,000, whereas during all these years they have been getting along on a basis of $3,000 from this Government, while Quebec judges have been getting $4,000 or $5,000 with a jurisdiction which may sound superior, but which I do not believe to be so in fact, outside of the few judges about whom the hon. member spoke. I think he

made a good case, if not for the present, at least for the future, for the principle I advocate, that a man ought to be paid for the work he does. To put a blanket figure over the whole Dominion of Canada for county and district judges of $5,000, $6,000, or $7,000, irrespective of the onus put upon them by work in their district or county, is a bad principle. In these times we should be careful; we are going on the basis of fixing salaries because of the high cost of living, but to-morrow the high cost of living may be the low cost of living; it certainly will, in a year or two, go down to normal conditions, and these judges, whose salaries we are fixing now on the basis of the high cost of living, will, during the rest of their lifetime, get the benefit of the figure fixed in war time at war prices, whereas if we wait a year or two, we would not fix it at all on the high cost of living. The Bill on the whole is to be commended, but I agree with the hon. member for Three Rivers (Mr. Bureau) that there are certain inequalities and inequitable conditions that ought to be specially taken up, I think, by a committee or by the minister (Mr. Doherty) when he returns, at a forthcoming session. The whole thing should then be gone into and ripped up and put on a common, practical, sound basis, so that a man should be paid for the work he does.
Mr. PRiOULX: On a few former occasions in this session requests have been made by some hon. members to increase the salaries of county court judges on account of the high cost of living, on the ground that their present salaries do not afford them a sufficient living allowance. I do not know that any request has been made to increase the salaries of Superior Court judges. As the hon. member for North 'Perth (Mr. IMorphy) has just said, we are fixing salaries now on the basis of the high cost of living. If that basis changes-and I believe it will soon change, because these are abnormal times- the salaries will be much higher than the cost of living would then warrant.
I submit that there was no necessity for increasing the salaries of the Superior Court judges just now; they could have waited for another year at least, particularly in view of the finances of the country. We have a very large deficit, and our expenditure is increasing, and I sympathize with the Minister of Finance who has to provide the money for all these increases. He must worry at times, and I think his sleep is interfered with occasionally when he sees all these increases mounting up.
I should like to know whether the Acting

Minister of Justice consulted him before drafting this resolution. I do not think he did, because I do not believe^ the Minister of Finance would have consented to these increases. There is another point we should consider, especially in connection with the Superior Court judges, and that is the question of retiring allowances. If you increase the judges' salaries, their retiring allowance is proportionately increased, and I think there have been abuses in the past in the matter of retiring allowances. There are some members of the bench who have retired after fifteen years' service in full physical and mental strength, and have gone back to their practice or taken up some other vocation while continuing to draw two-thirds of the salary they received while on the bench. Personally, I do not think a judge should be allowed to retire from the bench after fifteen years' service if his health is good enough to permit him to continue to serve on $ie bench. If he is invalided or incapable of performing his duties on account of old age, he could be allowed to retire, but I submit that we should change the law so that no judge shall be allowed to retire and draw the retiring allowance after fifteen years' service if he is in full physical and mental strength. I see by section 6 that the minister proposes to make a change. It provides :
That no annuity shall be granted to any judge under the provisions of sections 19 and 24 of the Judges Act relating to pensions and retirement unless the Governor in Council is of opinion that it is in the public interest that such judge should resign his office.
I do not like that provision very much, because it leaves too much discretion to the Governor in Council, and we know how that discretion has been exercised sometimes in the past by this and previous governments'. ^Et leaves the matter too much open to political influence, and I would like to see the provision changed so that a judge shall only draw his retiring allowance if he is incapacitated by reason of illness or old age. I think an age limit should also be fixed. We should not leave it to the discretion of the Governor in Council, because the Governor in Council is the Government and we know that Governments are often imposed upon by influential parties seeking favours. The judges are, in a sense, a privileged class, and we know that those who enjoy privileges sometimes ask for more. We have had experience of that in this country in connection with not only the manufacturing class but other classes also.
There is another question. The judges claim to be exempt from income taxation on account of constitutional limitations. We have passed an Act 'this session making judges appointed in the future liable to income taxation. The increases that are granted to the present judges will be exempt from taxation as their jsresent salaries are. I do not think that is fair, it is giving them undue privileges, and if this House is going to vote these increases in salary we should at least make the increases liable to federal taxation. There is another point. There is a difference of $1,000 in salary between the Chief Justice and the puisne judges; that is not new; it has existed for a long time, but I have never seen any reason for it. The Chief Justice does not do any more work than the puisne judges; sometimes he does less, and I think the honour of being Chief Justice should be sufficient.

speechtext: Will the honour of being Minister of Justice be sufficient?

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Some ministers do more work than others. As my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) has said, we should pay a man for the work he does. Now some puisne judges do more work than the 'Chief Justice, but receive $1,000 less salary I believe that is another privilege that should be abolished. This is the age of democracy, and everybody should be given a square deal; everybody should be paid for the work he does, 'but not more. 1 repeat that the honour of being Chief Justice should be sufficient without an additional $1,000
salary.	.
I have not much objection to the increase for the County Court judges, but as my hon. friend (Mr. Morphy) has said, there will be quite a few of them in Ontario who will be getting a large salary for doing little work. Provision has been made by the legislature for decreasing the number of County Court judges, but it will be some time before they are reduced to the required number. We cannot expect those in office to be patriotic enough to resign their positions. The legislature has also made provision for a special allowance of $1,000, and in some cases more than that, so" I submit that the County 'Court judges will be amply remunerated. I have less objection, however, to increasing their salaries than I have to increasing the salaries of the 'Superior Court judges at this time. There was no request from members of this House to increase the salaries of the Superior Court judges, and I believe they

could have waited longer, for another year at least.
Considering our comparatively small population in Canada, I think we should be very circumspect in the matter of the salaries paid our judges. It is true that in Great Britain the salaries of judges are higher than they are here, but each judge there has a jurisdiction over ten times the number of people that a judge in Canada has; and considering the number of the judges we have in this country I think we should be very sparing in the salaries we pay. We not only pay salaries to the judges while they are in office, but after fifteen years some judges retire on an allowance of two-thirds of their salaries, and after twenty-five years others retire on full pay. The public accounts will show that some judges receive $7,000 and $8,000 retiring allowance, and I know of one judge in Ontario who was receiving a salary of $7,000 and retired, not because he was incapacitated as a result of his duties; the law allowed him to retire on full salary; and now he is at the head of a large trust corporation and receives from' that corporation, in the way of salary, as much as his allowance, if not more. In the legal profession some men may receive larger incomes, but they have no retiring allowances; they themselves provide against old age. I am opposed to the principle of a retiring allowance for a judge unless he is incapacitated. With the salary he receives a judge can make provision, for the future. He can purchase an annuity the same as any member of the profession or a person in any other vocation; so that when old age overtakes him he may find himself provided for. If we are to continue the system of retiring allowances we should provide that judges should receive retiring allowances only when incapacitated through illness or old age, and we should not permit a judge to retire after fifteen years and resume practice or enter any other vocation while the country pays him a large retiring allowance.

speechtext:
My hon. friend from North Perth (Mr. Morphy) is often right in his contentions but sometimes he is wrong, and his argument of to-day comes under the latter description. I do not change my views in that regard, even when my friend is supported by the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx). His suggestion that the judges ought to be paid according to the amount of work that devolves upon them in. their own respective districts would be 
absolutely unworkable. It would involve a classification, and I suppose we would have to engage experts the same as we did in connection with the Civil Service. Such a classification, however, would be utterly impossible if fairness were to be aimed at. My hon. friend from North Perth is also wrong -when, he says that the county court judges of Ontario have absolutely the same work to perform as the judges of the Superior Court of Quebec in the rural districts. The mere fact that there are seventy-five judges of the county court in Ontario who administer justice in the rural distridts, while there are fifteen judges of the Superior Court of Quebec for the rural districts, shows that there is no similarity in their functions.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs

speechtext: That is not quite correct. The county court judges of Ontario exercise jurisdiction everywhere.

Even so, the difference in the number of judges-shows that they have not the same duties to perform.
I do not wish to repeat the argument I made at the opening of the discussion, but I must point out the anomaly that exists. You pay only $5,000 to each of fifteen judges of the higher court of Quebec having the same rank and jurisdiction as the judges of the cities of Montreal and Quebec, and those fifteen judges sit tour de role in review of the judgments rendered by the judges of Montreal and Quebec who are paid $2,000 more than they are.

speechtext: We have two sorts of appeal in civil cases in Quebec. There is the court of King's Bench sitting in appeal in all cases in which over $500 is involved, and there is the Court of Review, composed of judges of the Superior Court, sitting tour de role and called by the chief justice. They sit on appeals in cases under, as well as over, $500, because litigants have the right to inscribe their cases before the Court of Review as well as before the court of King's Bench, and the costs are much higher before the court of King's Bench than before the Court of Review.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

speechtext: You go from the Court of Review to the King's Bench?

In certain cases. When the judgment of the court of first instance is confirmed by the Court of Review you cannot go to the court of appeal; you have to go to the Supreme Court of Canada.

When the judgment of the court of first instance is reversed by the Court of Review, you have the right to appeal to the court of King's Bench. Therefore, you have this condition-which I wish to impress upon the minister-that the fifteen judges . of the Superior Court, which is the high court of Quebec, who are appointed for the rural districts, have to go to Montreal or Quebec and sit there in review of the judgments rendered by judges of the cities of Quebec and Montreal who are paid $2,000 more than men sitting on appeals from their own judgments,
That constitutes an absurd anomaly. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice pleads that in the absence of the Minister of Justice-who comes from the province of Quebec and who has been a judge of the province-he does not feel justified in making any change as to the Quebec conditions. Well, for the last few years the answer of the hon. Minister of Justice to the claims and complaints of the Quebec bar with regard to the change I am now advocating was that if he attempted to equalize the salaries of the Quebec judiciary, or to increase the salaries of some of the judges, it would open the door and he would have to increase the salaries of the judges in all the other provinces.

We have no representation in the present Government-we have nobody at the Council table to speak for our province. We do not complain at all-conditions will change. But we are here to have the views of the province heard, and I say that it is not fair when you are equalizing the salaries of the judges of the high courts in all the other provinces that you should ignore the judges in our own province. The minister says: "We want to give to the judges of the high courts of the other provinces the salaries that the judges have in Ontario and Quebec." Very well. The minister should have applied the same principle to some of the members of the high court of Quebec. In other words, if you equalize everywhere else you ought also to equalize in Quebec itself and place the fifteen judges of the high court on the same level as the twenty-one judges who have salaries of $7,000-on which basis the salaries of judges in the other provinces are now being adjusted by the proposed resolution.
My hon. friend has not said anything about the case of Mr. Justice Weir, to which I alluded at the opening of my remarks. This is a most glaring case. Four years ago the judge of the district of Pontiac, by an enactment of the Legislature of Quebec was compelled to remove to the city of Montreal and to sit there and administer justice in that district as well as in the district of Pontiac. He was not the only one affected; the judges of St. Hyacinthe, Beauharnois and Richelieu were also required to reside in Montreal and to administer justice in that district owing to the pressure of business there. Those three judges had their salaries increased the following year by the present Government-my hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice alluded to that a few minutes ago-'but the judge of the district of Pontiac was not given the increase of salary which was given to the three others. I do not know whether he applied for it or not. That is a most unfair discrimination. Nothing can be said against

Mr. Justice Weir personally. He was Speaker of the Legislature of Quebec for many years, he was provincial Minister of [DOT] Public Works for many years, and he was Provincial Treasurer for many years. Surely we are not going to let people believe that the political affiliations of members of the judiciary before their appointment ought to be considered when the question of salary is raised? But we are liable to make people believe that. There is no reason in the world why the judge of the district of Pontiac should not be placed on the same level as the other twenty-one judges who administer justice in the district of Montreal, and the whim of the Minister of Justice should not be the basis on which to make a readjustment of salaries.
My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice said that I had endorsed the demand of my hon. friend from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Mclsaac) that the three judges of the high court of that province should be given the same salary as the judges of the other provinces, and he added that this discrimination has always existed and that I -have approved of it. I have never been entrusted with the duty of readjusting the .salaries of the judiciary of the several provinces. Ther are two provinces in which the judges of the high courts are higher-salaried than the judges of the high courts in the other provinces. To-day, by this resolution, that anomaly disappears except as to the province of Prince Edward Island. I submit that this is not fair to the province. My hon. friend the Acting Minister of Justice says that the population is not so large as that of the other provinces. Well, that should not be taken into account. If three judges are too many for the administration of justice there, appoint only two, but pay them for their qualifications. They have to be as well, qualified, and to be of as high standing as the Judges of the other provinces, and the fact mentioned by my hon. friend from Kings (P.E.I.) that the present Chief Justice of Canada was a lawyer of Prince Edward Island, shows that the legal men of that province have at least the same standing and* the same qualifications as their confreres in the other provinces. But I say that the moment you introduce a law to equalize the salaries of the judges of the high courts of this country, you should put them all on the same level,- the fifteen judges of the province of Quebec as well as the three judges of Prince Edward Island who are at present being discriminated against.

speechtext: I would like to say a word, Mr. Chairman, with reference to the point raised by yourself in connection with the exemption from income tax of the salaries of the judges.
