If it is, then I submit it should be dealt with. When the income tax Bill was before the House the point was raised, and perhaps rightly so, that so far as the judges already appointed are concerned there was really a contractual relationship between them and the country. That is that they accepted the positions which they occupy under the law as it stood at the time of their appointment. That would possibly give them what has been termed so frequently in the House of late, a vested right. Whether that vested right is any higher than the right of municipalities and of provinces, about which we heard so much yesterday in connection with the Railway Bill and which the altered condition of affairs was felt to give to the Parliament of Canada the right to interfere with, is not a matter which I intend to discuss today. The income tax law has at least established this: That judges hereafter appointed will be liable to the payment of income tax, and if that is so it seems to me that the point raised by the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) was well taken. That is, that if the relationship between this Parliament or the country, and the judges already appointed is changed by increasing the remuneration to which they were entitled at the time of their appointment, and if that is based, as the minister has explained, on the high cost of living, then I submit to the House it would be fair to assume that part of the high cost of living of to-day is the income tax which people are obliged to pay. if it is right to impose on men earning $1,000 a year an income tax and the tendency is downward- the tendency is to reduce the exemption rather .than increase it-then I submit that the judges, particularly those whose remuneration is being increased should be made liable to income tax, and it should apply to those already appointed and who fire having their salaries increased. The income tax in such cases should apply not merely to the amount of the increase but to the whole of the salary received. I submit further to the Acting Minister of Justice that the Government should take

into consideration the question of placing all the members of the Bench upon such a salary basis as would enable them to pay their share of the income tax the same as other people. I think it is unfortunate that the law as it stands should make it possible in this House, as well as in the press and in the country, to be continually referring to the fact that the judges on the bench are not contributing the same as other people in the way of income tax. This position is particularly important under the conditions as they exist to-day. Now, if it is felt that the law as it existed at the time of their appointment should exempt judges for all time from the payment of income tax, then it would be a good thing for the general conditions in the country if the salaries of the judges were put upon a basis that would enable them, or would justify the country in coming back and assessing them the same as all other members of the community for their fair share of the income tax.	,

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I desire very cordially to endorse what the hon. gentleman (Mr. J. A. Stewart) has said, and what you yourself, Sir, speaking from your seat a while ago, said on this question of exemption. I offered a suggestion a few days since on the same lines.
I presumed that these resolutions had been drafted before that, otherwise it seemed to me the suggestion was so natural and proper that the minister would have provided for it. When the tax exemption privilege was embodied in the Judges Act there were no direct taxes imposed in this country, and consequently we were giving the judges no favour or consideration; there was no such tax to be exempted from. If ait the time the income tax was applied it had been made to apply to judges as well, there really would not have been any very serious breach of faith, because you would not have been imposing upon them something in regard to which they had been previously exempted. But the view was taken, and I concurred in it myself, that there was some contractual relationship between Parliament and the judges, as said by my hon. friend (Mr. Stewart); I was one of those who thought we should not interfere with the rights under that relationship, although some hon. gentlemen held a different view. However, another Income Tax Bill for the present year has provided that as respects all judges appointed hereafter they shall be liable for income tax. That is a very proper step to take. Now I
want to respectfully urge upon the Acting Minister of Justice that he put a clause in this Bill that as respects all the judges whose salaries are increased by it, they shall not get the benefit oi that"exemption.
If they have a vested right in the exemption, they have not a vested right in the increase, and I submit that they should not have both the exemption and the increase,
I therefore hope that before the minister gets his Bill through he will insert a clause providing that. as respects those to whom an increase of salary is given they shall not be exempt from income tax. Surely, there can hardly be any division of opinion in that respect. I would like also to concur in the view which the member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) expressed with regard to the retirement of judges on pensions. There has been a good deal of fine pleading as to the meaning of the provision in the existing law respecting the retirement of judges. We all recognize that the basic principle of any pension to a public servant is that he is only entitled to a pension when he can no longer discharge his duties. When he has arrived at an advanced age -and that age is fixed at seventy-five-it might in fairness be said that he has a right to his retirement; but up to that time, so long as he is physically and mentally able to discharge his duties,
I claim he has no right to a pension at all. And, if he is to receive a pension to suit his convenience, or to suit some party convenience, or to make a place for somebody else, all I can say is that that is an evasion of the true principle of a pension. I would therefore strongly urge the minister to consider, in dealing with the annuity clause, making provision for the retirement of a judge when he reaches an advanced age, because only in such a case should a judge have any right of retirement unless he is physically or mentally disqualified for the performance of his duties.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Before dealing with the points raised by the hon. members who have just spoken I will refer to what has been said by hon. gentlemen opposite regarding the province of Quebec. I would not like any hon. member to be so influenced by the persistency of the presentation by my hon. friends opposite as Ito feel there was really discrimination against the province of Quebec in this Bill, because such does not exist. If what these hon. gentlemen are asking for were to be done it would mean that any province in Con-

federation that chose to denominate all its courts "Superior" courts, no matter what class of cases they try-though they went from the top right down to the lowest class of cases tried-must as a result receive the maximum salary of the highest court of any otner province that classifies its jurisdiction. That is their argument, there can be no escape from it.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: That is not the argument at all.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Then there is no argument on my hon. friend's part.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The argument is that you are discriminating because you do not equalize the salaries in Quebec as you do in other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: We do not Taise them all to the maximum in every other province.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Of the same jurisdiction, you do.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
There is only one jurisdiction in Quebec; the courts have the same jurisdiction throughout. If an addition were made to-day to the salaries of all the judges in the province of Quebec, it would be found that those salaries would be well up

-Mr. BUREAU: You are discriminating to the extent of $134,000 in favour of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Ontario is larger than other provinces.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: You are paying more for your judges in Ontario in proportion to population.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I had not given close attention to this phase of the question because I believed that the ground I was standing on was sound. But counting the judges of the province one by one, I make a total of fifty-one Superior Court judges in Quebec, inclusive of four Circuit Court judges, who receive, I understand, $4,000 a year. There is nothing like that in any other province.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: You have seventy-two County Court judges in Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Yes, but a very small Superior Court Bench. If my hon. friend's argument is sound, it means that any province that chooses not to classify its jurisdiction, or chooses to extend the jurisdiction of its King's Bench, its Superior Court, right from the highest to the lowest, is then entitled to call upon the Dominion Treasury

to give to the entire Bench of that province the maximum salary provided for any other province.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: You cannot twist it about to make an argument of that kind.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: There is no twisting at all.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: There is; I will show it to you.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Show it to me now.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Go on; finish your argument.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
There are no intermediate jurisdictions in Quebec, as there are in Ontario and Manitoba. The great majority of the cases that are tried in Ontario and Manitoba-there are few of the very large cases; the majority involve only such amounts as $1,000, $500 and down-are tried by the County Court judges, whereas in Quebec they ar-e tried by the Superior Court judges. What will be the result if all the Superior Court judges of that province are to get the maximum salary given to the judge of a Court of Appeal in Ontario? This will indicate the real nature of the argument made by hon. gentlemen, although they put it this way: Do not discriminate between Three Rivers and the rural districts of Quebec. In view of the course that has been followed, I know of no other way of overcoming the difficulty inherent in the fact that the constitution of the courts of the province of Quebec differs from the constitution of the courts in other provinces.
I do not argue that as time advances additions should not be made to the salaries of judges Who receive the higher remuneration. It may be that Three Rivers has advanced to the point where it is so entitled; it may be that one or two other points have also arrived at that point; I do not know. Of that others are better qualified to judge than I am. But to say that all salaries should be raised, as has been suggested, is to argue against the plain facts, is to argue something that would result in an absurdity if the suggestion was adopted. On scarcely a single occasion when the Judges -Act has been changed in recent years has the door not been opened that hon. gentlemen have talked about and additions made to the Bench of the province of Quebec and to the salaries of judges there. I do not think the Judges 'Act has been amended once since I have been in this House without that being done; so that it is unfair for hon. gentle- [DOT] men opposite to try to persuade members

of the House who are not so well acquainted with conditions as they are, that there is anything in the nature of discrimination here, or that there ever has: been anything of that nature. The facts are all against that argument.
The subject of income tax is one to which I have not given special attention in connection with this measure. The purpose of this Bill is not to raise a revenue but to increase the salaries of some of the lesser paid and more deserving judges of the country. It is true that by striking out a clause of the Judges Act so far as it is applicable to those now receiving an increase of remuneration, an addition to the revenue could be made. But would that be fair? I see some objections to it; at all events there are some things that should be taken into account. If the income tax provision of the Judges Act is. made applicable from now on to all judges whose salaries are increased by the present resolution there will still be discrimination between those whose salaries are raised and put on a level with others and those whose salaries have always been at the level to which this former class approaches. I believe that the Income Tax Act which was passed this session provides that as to future appointments, judges shall be liable to that tax. It would appear to me that whatever is done would be better done by amendment to the Judges Act. I do not like the idea- of selecting certain judges who are already on the Bench and making them liable to income tax while certain other judges who are on the Bench and who have received higher salaries all along are not liable. It seems to me that for all it is worth, it would give rise to certain heartburnings on the part of those who have had the lower salaries all these years. At the same time, I realize that the argument that has hitherto prevailed, namely, that to exact a tax after appointment is in a measure a breach of faith, does not apply so strongly, if at all, to those whose salaries are at the same time increased. But chiefly for the reason that taxes are better dealt with by a Tax Bill, it occurs to me that the better way to arrive at the same result would be to make such amendments to the Income Tax Act this session or next session as may be considered equitable all round.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Would it be possible to
make such amendments to the Income Tax Act without breaking faith with the judges?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Well, so far as breaking faith goes, it would be exactly the
same under the Income Tax Act as under this Act. But I do not think there would be anything in the way of breaking faith, no matter how it was done.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: If it were not for the special exemption provisions of this Act, would the salaries not come under the Income Tax law without any special amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Oh, yes.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Then I submit
that the taking away of this exemption would not make it a matter of raising revenue; we are simply taking away an impediment to the raising of revenue.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: But by the Income Tax Act we take away an impediment already as regards future appointees; we simply state that notwithstanding this provision, the Income Tax Act shall apply in the case of future appointments. There is no reason ,why, if it is considered just, there should not be an amendment to provide that it should apply all round, or that it should apply in the case of all whose salaries were increased by the present Bill. What I argue is that it is better done by the Income [DOT]Tax Act than by this measure.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
If my hon. friend adheres to that view, it means this, that it will not be done at all, whereas, by this suggestion, it will be done. I cannot understand the logic of my hon. friend when he says that it cannot be done in this Bill; that it ought to be done in an Income Tax Bill. The exemption provision is not in the Income Tax Bill; but in the Judges Act, and if it is right and legitimate in the law of the country to have the exemption in the Judges Act, what can be wrong in dealing with abolishing the exemption in the present Bill? Surely my hon. friend can see that his argument in this respect must fail. This is the right time and place to do this. It is a condition we attach to the increase of salary. I am not opposing the increase in salary; I am strongly of the opinion that the judges of the country should be generously paid, so that they may be able to uphold their dignity in the matter of their financial position and in other respects, and if the impression goes abroad that the judges of the country are going to be exempted from these burdens we do not increase the respect for the judiciary. There will, indeed, be a disposition to complain and grumble and say: While the common man in the country is taxed, the well-paid judge is not taxed. Therefore, I think my

hon. friend's argument is not strong in that respect. Then he says: There will be discrimination. We have already discriminated in respect to the future, so that there is a good precedent. There will be some discrimination in any case. The judges whose salaries are not increased by this Bill will still be exempted from tax. I would be very glad to remove the exemption altogether,-except that that would be regarded as a breach of faith. But we must be practical. If the minister approves the suggestion which has been brought forward by the hon. members for Lanark (Mr. Stewart), and Prescott (Mr. Proulx) and myself, he should deal with this matter in this Bill, and the amendment would come properly as an amendment to the Judges Act. I would strongly urge the minister to take this into consideration before the Bill reaches its final stages, and that he draft an amendment.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The point, as I stated, was brought to my attention only last night, I think, and I have not had time to give it any thought since. I realize that what the hon. member says is right, that it would be impracticable now to amend the Income Tax Act. That is quite true. But it could be done next session and made applicable just the same, and there would be no difference whatever in the amount of the taxes collected. The question is only one of method. On principle, I am not opposed to the suggestion at all; I approve it; I do not think there should be any exception from income tax at all to judges or to anybody else; and the argument as to breach of contract makes little or no impression on my mind.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
There is no breach of
contract in what I suggest.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I realize that. As regards the resolution, there is no need of anything being contained in the resolution as to the amendment of the exemption clause of the Judges Act. There would be no need of a resolution to that effect at all. The Bill that will be introduced may contain a clause modifying the exemption, if it is thought fit to do so, without any reference to it in the resolutions whatever. Therefore, I suggest that the resolutions pass in their present form, be put through their readings, and I will give consideration to a modification of the exemption clause in the Bill that will be brought down as a result.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
Before that is done, I should like to make one suggestion 
with regard to what the minister has said. It would be a mistake, providing that we are doing away with exemption, to adopt the form he suggests of having that exemption referred to in the Income Tax Act rather than in this; for this reason, that a vested right is established here if we pass this Bill as suggested; and we have no moral right to do away with that vested right; the contract is just as binding on us for the additional $1,000 as it was for the former amount.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The man is already appointed.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
There is no
reason why we should do a thing a wrong way instead of a right way. If we are to do it at all, the right way is certainly to do it in this Bill. I, therefore, think it well to suggest that to the minister before we get past the resolution stage, so that he may bear the matter in mind.
As regards the question of increased salaries and those salaries being based upon the high cost of living, I cannot agree with the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Proulx) at all. The present proposed salaries are not based on the high cost of living; if they were based on that, they should be very much higher. It is an outrage that the salaries have not been in creased before this, and if any change is to be made, the increase should be greater rather than less. We are not going in the future to get the class of judges we want unless we pay them according to the services we expect them to render. If we expect to get the very best men, the only way to get them is to pay them properly. Even if the cost of living does decrease very greatly, the salaries will still not be any too high.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
I would prefer to see this exemption taken out and see it in the Tax Bill, because these judges are already appointed, and they may, therefore, contend that when they were appointed they were not subject to taxation, and that this increase is no more liable to taxation than their present salaries. As regards the question of discrimination against those appointed in the future, they are not compelled to accept the position; if they are not willing to accept the salary because it is liable to income tax, they need not accept it. It would be much better to provide for the exemption in the Income Tax Act.
M. BUREAU: The acting minister has just read a letter from the Chief Justice in

Montreal with reference to the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier (Mr. Jacobs). It would be unfair to let this letter go on Hansard as read, without calling the attention of the committee to the fact that, subsequently to the statement made by that hon. member in this House, he rose in his place and gave an explanation and asked to have Hansard correct the report as Hansard had not reported him Tightly. I note that in the letter-I am subject to correction-the words put into the mouth of the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier are "the last five judges appointed." The hon. member corrected that and stated that it should be "some of the judges appointed," instead of "the last five judges appointed." The wording "the last five judges appointed" just exactly puts the finger on a certain number of judges to whom he did not want to allude at all and who did not belong to the category of judges of whom he was then speaking. On the 19th of June, as reported on Hansard, page 3845, the hon. member for George Etienne Cartier said:
Hansard has me reported as saying " five " judges instead of " some " judges, and as a result X understand that five of the most recently appointed gentlemen have taken this to mean that my remarks were intended to apply to them. These judges are: Justices Allard. Tellier, Duclos, DeLorimier and Loranger. I wish to say that I did not have in mind any of these gentlemen. They are expeditious in the handling of their cases.
And so on. He explains the whole situation. I say this in justice to that hon. gentleman so that nobody will remain under the impression that he was still subject to the corrections contained in the letter which the minister read, and that he did not make any explanation to the House.
The minister states that we have allowed this matter of judges' salaries to pass from year to year when the Estimates were going through, and that, in the absence of the Minister of Justice, he does not want to take the matter up. Hansard will show that year after year I have raised this question of discrimination against the judges of the rural districts in the province of Quebec, and that the present Minister of Justice has stated: We do not want to open the question at this time because it would mean that we would have to equalize the salaries of the judges all over the Dominion, but when the matter comes up your request will be taken into consideration. He admitted, as the Acting Minister of Justice has admitted, that I had a good case. You may say that the district
of Three Rivers is an isolated case. I speak of Three Rivers because I practise there, and I know all the ins and outs of the judicial system in that district.. From hearsay, and from the general expansion of business that has taken place, I would judge that the same might be said of Sherbrooke, and the district of St. Francis, but I could not give details in those cases because I do not practise there. I know, however, that water-powers are being developed on the St. Francis river and case after case is decided in that district of the same kind as are decided in the district of Three Rivers. I plead for Three Rivers not because the district is exceptional, but simply because it is the district where I practise and I know everything about judicial matters there. The reasoning of my hon. friend-what I call the twist-is this: He assumes that all that need be done to get a salary of $7,000, is for the province to say: W'e will consider all the judges as belonging to the Superior Court. Is that correct?

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I said that that would be required to be done if the argument presented was sound.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
At the time of confederation there were judicial systems established in the province of Quebec and Ontario and those systems, it was taken for granted, would continue on the same basis, with this modification, that the number of judges required to administer justice under those systems should be increased as required by the development of either province. When this matter was discussed the Fathers of Confederation knew very well that we had one court of unlimited jurisdiction. They knew on the other hand that Ontario had county court judges. My hon. friend wants to give the impression to the committee that all the province has to do is to legislate. But that is not all the province has to do. We have the right to create additional judgeships, but we cannot fill them until the Federal Government says it is necessary to make the appointments. No legislation can be taken seriously that would destroy the basis upon which confederation was established. No reasonable man would judge the standing of a court simply by the name which the Provincial Legislature chose to give to that court. It was not because the judges bore a certain name that their salaries were fixed; it was on account of the very foundation of the judicial system which existed in the provinces at the time of Confederation. This is the system that has existed

with us. The test to apply is very easy. Take the population of Ontario and the population of Quebec, and see how much it costs to administer justice in the respective provinces. I venture to say that the cost of administering justice in the province of Quebec is no higher than the cost of administering justice in the province of Ontario, and if this legislation is passed the cost of administering justice in the province of Quebec is going to be less than in the province of Ontario. I shall refer to these figures again in the House. What I am objecting to now is the fact that my hon. friend proceeds on a hypothesis which is not reasonable. It is not reasonable to suppose that by changing the name of a court you change the functions of that court.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I said, change the jurisdiction, make it unlimited.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Change the jurisdiction, if you will; that makes no difference at all. I do not know what the jurisdiction of the county courts in Ontario is, but you have seventy-two judges there to look after these cases at a salary of $3,000 each, and it is now proposed to increase their salaries by $1,000 each. The combined salaries are $288,000, at $4,000 each, or $216,000 at $3,000 each.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Before any attempt was made to increase the salaries, a letter was addressed to the Attorney-General of the province of Ontario, and a request was made that provision bp made for reducing the bench of Ontario, because we were convinced that it was much larger than there was any need for. That provision was made and is going into effect now; it is partially in effect already, because certain judges have passed away, and there are several vacancies in Ontario now. It will go into effect continuously, until the number will be reduced to forty-five.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:
We do not ask for any reduction. You were willing to pay those judges in Ontario whether there was work for them or not. You cannot decrease the number of judges in the province of Que-bee because we have hardly enough now for the work there is to do. If it is necessary to put aside so many judges in the province of Ontario there must have been something wrong in the appointing of these judges, or with the legislature. Of course, I know nothing about it, but perhaps the reason is that Ontario is going backwards so far as litigation is concerned; I should be sorry to see that. But that does not

affect our system. You paid this money whether services were rendered or not, and I thinik if you reduced the number of county court judges in Ontario by half you would not be any worse [DOT] off. It is not a question of name or jurisdiction, but a question of carrying on the work of the country. I say that the judges in the province of Quebec who reside outside of the cities of Montreal and Quebec "are treated with discrimination in the matter of salary. I am not asking for any increase in salary. My point is this: Here are these men doing just as much work, more work in fact, being handicapped in the exercise of their functions. They have not the same facilities and the same advantages as the judges who get the higher salaries; and we ask that they be put on the same footing. The answer is: No, the Minister of Justice is not here. That is not fair. I for one feel that in the interests of the country I should not vote for the resolution as it stands, although I want to be understood that I am in favour of everything in it; but what is omitted from it I consider just as important, if not more important, as a matter of equity and justice than what it contains.
These men have to keep up a higher standard of living than men of ordinary rank, and I do not see why, when every one else from the foot of the social ladder to the top is being increased, these particular persons should not also receive increases, if for no other reason ithan the high cost of living. Our legal system as regards salaries was established at Confederation and has not changed. The salaries were based on conditions existing then, but conditions have changed considerably. Can my hon. friend tell me why it is thalt the judge for the district of Pontiac, when conditions are absolutely the same in every detail as those of St. Hyacinthe, Beauharnois and Richelieu, should not be put on the same footing and his salary increased to $7,000 the same as the others? This man is just as qualified, and the only reason that will appeal to any rational man is that the discrimination is made on account of his political activities and clashes that he may have had with the present Minister of Justice in former years.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Is that Mr. Justice Weir?

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I must say that I did not know, until I heard the hon. member speak, what the political proclivities of that gentleman were.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I told you a few minutes ago that he had been provincial treasurer of Quebec, and speaker of the legislature, and had been active in politics.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Well, I did not catch that remark when it was made. The hon. gentleman is quite wrong in that regard. The only reason was that I did not think it was for me as Acting Minister of Justice to pass upon the relative merits and duties of judges of Quebec. If it had been a matter of general increases all round I should have put it into the Bill; but as it was a matter of a particular advancement I thought it was more appropriate to leave it to the minister.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Every province receives the benefit of the Bill except Quebec. My hon. friend just now said-when the member for Kamouraska made the statement that it was because we were not represented -that the latch string was out. We do not want to have any string on this Government, nor do we want the Government (to have any string on us. We do not complain about not being represented. We just present our case on its merits and urge the fairness of it. Whatever the reasons may be, the conclusions have to be drawn by every member of the House and every individual outside. It can be shown by Hansard that the Minister of Jusltice (Mr. Doherty) has always said that when the general revision of judges' salaries was made this matter would be taken into consideration. My hon. friend took it up this session for the purpose of availing himself of the excuse that might exist that the Minister of Justice being from Quebec, he would leave it to him to decide this question. If he brought the matter up to take advantage of that excuse, I can draw my own conclusions. On the other hand, the hon. gentleman knows very well that the Minister of Justice, or any Minister of Justice, wTill not open up the question of judges' salaries for the purpose of dealing with one province.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I am very anxious that this resolution should go through, and if there is any further discussion it can be had on the Bill. As far as I am concerned, the resolution has some disappointments for me, but taking it all in all it is not. so very bad. I hope the resolution will be permitted to go through to-night.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext:

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: The Bill will be up and will have three readings, and there will be the committee stage.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: It has not been the custom this session, at least so far, to have a discussion on the second reading of a Bill. The Bill is just read the second time and the House goes into committee on it, and you cannot discuss certain matters when you are going through the Bill clause by clause. My -hon. friend the minister and other lawyers know better than others that when you discuss a Bill in Committee you are bound by the rules to confine yourself to the clause under consideration. On second reading you have to discuss the principle of the Bill and keep to generalities. We are in favour of the principle of the Bill, but the only time you can have a discussion such as would cover the matters hon. members desire to deal with is on the resolution.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I am supporting the passing of the resolution on the understanding that whatever any hon. member has to say can be said later on.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Our point is that the judges of Quebec should be given the same increase, to equalize their salaries, with those of other judges. That cannot be done except by way of resolution before the introduction of the Bill. If the resolution is permitted to pass we shall be precluded from changing the Bill in that respect, and to remedy the matter another resolution would have to be introduced.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: If this resolution passes the hon. gentleman will be quite free when the Bill is under consideration to move an amendment if he chooses.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: You could not increase the salaries-.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: We will not fall into your trap.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: There will be no trap.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: You cannot increase the salaries without a resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: If hon. gentlemen have any doubts I am prepared to continue now and hear the amendment so that the committee can pass upon it. Hon. gentlemen have spoken all afternoon and presented no amendment. We have made no progress-, but have had a repetition of one phase of the argument.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: Thank you. That is very fair on the part of the minister.

maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: We can carry it over to Monday.

speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
maintopic: SCHOOL AND DOMINION LANDS IN TABER IRRIGATION DISTRICT.
speechtext: I am prepared to go on now. My recollection is that we were not to sit to-night, but I am prepared to stay.
